hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: The yellow sheet lists milli- as 10 −3 and nano- as 10 −9 , so 1 mm = 10 −3 m and 1 ng = 10 −9 g. Rewrite each equality in whole-number form.
hints.answer: 1000 mm = 1 m (because 1 ÷ 10 −3 = 1000), and 10 9 ng = 1 g (because 1 ÷ 10 −9 = 10 9 ).
hints.hint: Divide both sides of each equality by the power of ten so the prefixed unit has a whole-number count.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{21}\)
hints.question: A cup of yogurt is labeled 6.0 oz. What is its mass in grams? (1 g = 0.03527 oz)
hints.answer: \( 6.0\ \text{oz} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{g}}{0.03527\ \text{oz}} = 170.1\ \text{g} \to \) 1.7 × 10 2 g (2 significant figures, from 6.0 oz; "170 g" also shows 2 under this book's rule).
hints.hint: Use 1 g = 0.03527 oz with ounces on the bottom so they cancel. A gram is much smaller than an ounce, so the number of grams must be larger.

hints.title: Problem 1.78
hints.question: A student finds an unlabeled bottle of clear liquid in the stockroom and forms the hypothesis "This liquid is ethanol (density 0.789 g/mL)." She measures three different volumes of the liquid. Her data are in the table below. Mass and volume of three samples of an unknown liquid Trial Volume (mL) Mass (g) 1 20.0 15.8 2 15.0 11.8 3 25.0 19.7 (a) Calculate the density for each trial. (b) Do the data support her hypothesis? (c) The volumes were different, so why are the densities nearly the same? (d) Do the data prove the liquid is ethanol? Suggest one more physical property she could measure.
hints.answer: (a) Trial 1: 15.8 g ÷ 20.0 mL = 0.790 g/mL . Trial 2: 11.8 g ÷ 15.0 mL = 0.787 g/mL (calculator: 0.78667). Trial 3: 19.7 g ÷ 25.0 mL = 0.788 g/mL . (b) Yes. All three values are within 0.002 g/mL of ethanol's 0.789 g/mL. (c) Density is intensive . A larger sample has proportionally more mass and more volume, so the ratio stays the same. The small differences come from normal measurement limits. (d) No. The data support the hypothesis but do not prove it; another liquid could have a similar density. Measuring a second intensive property, such as the boiling point (ethanol boils at 78 °C), would be a stronger test. If both match, she can be much more confident. This is the scientific method at work: test a hypothesis more than one way.
hints.hint: (a) Divide mass by volume for each trial. (b) Compare with 0.789 g/mL. (c) Density is intensive. (d) One property can match by chance; what other characteristic property could she measure?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{8}\)
hints.question: Choose a sensible metric unit for each: (a) the mass of a newborn; (b) the amount of vitamin B 12 in one tablet; (c) the diameter of a red blood cell; (d) the volume of an IV bag.
hints.answer: (a) kg (newborns are about 3 to 4 kg). (b) mcg (micrograms; vitamin B 12 doses on labels are written in micrograms). (c) µm (micrometers; a red blood cell is about 7 to 8 µm across). (d) mL or L (common bags hold 250 mL to 1 L). A good unit keeps the number between about 0.1 and 1000.
hints.hint: Think about the size of each thing: pick the prefix that gives a number that is not too large or too small (a newborn is a few of which unit?).

hints.title: Problem 1.75
hints.question: A science-night demonstrator drops a chunk of dry ice (solid CO 2 , density about 1.5 g/cm 3 ) into a bowl of warm water. It bubbles, and a thick white fog rolls over the rim of the bowl. First, the white fog is mostly: A. carbon dioxide gas B. tiny droplets of liquid water condensed from water vapor in the air that the very cold CO 2 gas chilled C. smoke from the dry ice burning D. hydrogen and oxygen gas from water breaking apart Then answer: (e) Does the dry ice sink or float? (f) Name the change of state the dry ice undergoes. (g) Classify CO 2 as an element, compound, or mixture. (h) Are the bubbles evidence of a chemical change?
hints.answer: B. Carbon dioxide gas is colorless and invisible. The very cold CO 2 gas chills the moist air above the bowl, and the water vapor condenses into tiny droplets that you see as fog (the same physical change that makes tule fog). A is wrong: CO 2 gas is invisible, so it cannot be the white fog. C is wrong: nothing is burning; there is no flame and no new substance. D is wrong: breaking water into hydrogen and oxygen is a chemical change that warm water and dry ice do not cause. (e) Sinks: about 1.5 g/cm 3 is greater than water's 1.00 g/mL (1 cm 3 = 1 mL). (f) Sublimation (solid → gas), a physical change. (g) Compound: carbon and oxygen bonded in a fixed 1:2 ratio. (h) No. The bubbles are CO 2 gas from the dry ice subliming, and the CO 2 was already there as a solid. A gas forming is only a clue to a chemical change; here no new substance forms.
hints.hint: Carbon dioxide gas is colorless. What visible thing forms when very cold gas chills moist air? For (e)–(h), compare densities, name the solid-to-gas change, and ask whether any new substance forms.

hints.title: Problem 1.45
hints.question: Which pair of particles repels? A. Mg 2+ and Cl − B. a proton and an electron C. F − and O 2− D. Li + and Br −
hints.answer: C. Both particles are negative, and like charges repel. (The sizes of the charges differ, but only the signs decide attract or repel.) A: positive and negative attract. B: a proton is positive and an electron is negative, so they attract. D: positive and negative attract.
hints.hint: Only the signs decide attract or repel: opposite signs attract, like signs repel. Which pair has the same sign?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Will a fluoride ion, F − , attract or repel (a) a potassium ion, K + ; (b) a chloride ion, Cl − ?
hints.answer: (a) attract (opposite signs); (b) repel (both negative).
hints.hint: Opposite signs attract; like signs repel. Compare the sign of F<sup>−</sup> with each ion.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: Identify the number and the unit: (a) 250 mL; (b) 4.1 mmol/L of potassium; (c) one dozen syringes.
hints.answer: (a) 250, milliliters. (b) 4.1, millimoles per liter (a combined unit). (c) 1, dozen syringes (a counted unit; one dozen is exactly 12).
hints.hint: A measurement has a number and a unit. Combined units (like "per liter") and counted units (like dozen) count as units too.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: A problem says, "A 12.0 oz can of soda contains 34.0 mg of caffeine." Write the conversion factor both ways up, and say which one you would use to find the caffeine in 3 cans (36.0 oz).
hints.answer: 34.0 mg caffeine / 12.0 oz soda, or 12.0 oz soda / 34.0 mg caffeine. To go from ounces to milligrams, ounces must be on the bottom: 36.0 oz × (34.0 mg / 12.0 oz) = 102 mg caffeine .
hints.hint: Write the factor both ways up. To go from ounces to milligrams, which version has ounces on the bottom?

hints.title: Problem 1.72
hints.question: A Lodi winery lab measures out a 250. mL sample of wine to test. The wine's density is 0.993 g/mL. What is the mass of the sample?
hints.answer: You start with milliliters and want grams, so use the density with mL on the bottom: \( 250.\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{0.993\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mL}} = 248.25\ \text{g} \) The decimal point in 250. mL means three significant figures, and 0.993 g/mL has three, so the mass is 248 g . Check: the density is just under 1 g/mL (the alcohol in wine is less dense than water), so the mass in grams is just under the volume in milliliters.
hints.hint: Start with the volume that stands alone and use the density with mL on the bottom so milliliters cancel.

hints.title: Problem 1.29
hints.question: Which of these is a compound? A. O 3 (ozone) B. N 2 C. NH 3 (ammonia) D. air
hints.answer: C. NH 3 contains two different elements, nitrogen and hydrogen, bonded in a fixed 1:3 ratio. A is an element: every atom in O 3 is oxygen. A subscript does not make a compound. B is an element (one of the diatomic seven): only one kind of atom. D is a homogeneous mixture of several gases (mostly N 2 and O 2 ), not one substance.
hints.hint: A compound has two or more different elements bonded together in a fixed ratio. A subscript alone does not make a compound, and a mixture is not a substance.

hints.title: Problem 1.7
hints.question: Classify each statement as a scientific law, a scientific theory, or a hypothesis. (a) Matter is made of particles that are always moving, and the faster they move, the hotter the sample. (b) Every sample of pure water, from any source, contains hydrogen and oxygen in the same proportion by mass. (c) If I put a heat lamp in this chicken coop, the hens will lay more eggs this month. (d) The total mass of a sealed bottle containing water and an antacid tablet is the same before and after the tablet fizzes.
hints.answer: (a) Theory. It explains why samples are hot or cold, using a model of moving particles. (b) Law. It describes what always happens, based on many measurements, without explaining why. (c) Hypothesis. It is a testable prediction about one situation that has not been tested yet. (d) Law. It is an example of the law of conservation of mass: in a closed container, mass before a change equals mass after. (The bottle must be sealed; if the gas escaped, the measured mass would drop.)
hints.hint: A law states what always happens (often from measurements); a theory explains why with a model; a hypothesis is a testable prediction about one situation.

hints.title: Problem 2.4
hints.question: In Thomson's cathode-ray tube, the glowing beam bent toward a positively charged plate. What did this show? A. The beam was made of negatively charged particles. B. The beam was made of positively charged particles. C. Atoms have a small, dense nucleus. D. The beam was made of neutral particles.
hints.answer: A. Opposite charges attract (Section 1.7), so a beam pulled toward a positive plate must carry negative charge. Those particles are electrons. B is backward: positive particles would be pushed away from a positive plate. C is the conclusion of Rutherford's gold foil experiment, not Thomson's cathode-ray experiment. D cannot be right: neutral particles are not pulled by either plate, so the beam would go straight.
hints.hint: Opposite charges attract (Section 1.7). What charge must the beam carry to be pulled toward a positive plate?

hints.title: Problem 2.22
hints.question: Which set contains only metalloids? A. B, Si, As B. C, Si, Ge C. Al, Si, P D. Si, Ge, Sn
hints.answer: A. Boron, silicon, and arsenic all sit along the staircase line. B includes carbon, a nonmetal. C includes aluminum, a metal, and phosphorus, a nonmetal. D includes tin, a metal. Silicon and germanium are metalloids, but group 14 changes from nonmetal (C) to metalloids (Si, Ge) to metals (Sn, Pb) as you go down.
hints.hint: Metalloids lie along the staircase: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te. Check every element in each set; one non-metalloid rules a set out.

hints.title: Problem 2.26
hints.question: Complete the table below for monatomic ions. Monatomic ions to complete (blanks marked ?) Ion symbol Ion name Protons Electrons Charge Li + ? ? ? ? Ba 2+ ? ? ? ? Se 2− ? ? ? ? ? iodide ? ? ? ? ? 15 18 ? ? ? 38 ? 2+
hints.answer: Protons = Z. Electrons = protons − charge. Charge = protons − electrons. Li + : lithium ion ; 3 protons, 3 − 1 = 2 electrons; charge 1+. Ba 2+ : barium ion ; 56 protons, 56 − 2 = 54 electrons; charge 2+. Se 2− : selenide ; 34 protons, 34 + 2 = 36 electrons; charge 2−. Iodide: I − ; 53 protons, 54 electrons; charge 1−. 15 protons is phosphorus; charge = 15 − 18 = 3− , so the ion is P 3− , phosphide . 38 protons is strontium: Sr 2+ , strontium ion ; 38 − 2 = 36 electrons . Every charge matches the group pattern: Li (group 1) 1+, Ba and Sr (group 2) 2+, P (group 15) 3−, Se (group 16) 2−, I (group 17) 1−. Cations keep the element name; anions end in -ide.
hints.hint: Use protons = Z, electrons = protons − charge, and charge = protons − electrons. Name metal cations "___ ion" and nonmetal anions with -ide.

hints.title: Problem 2.5
hints.question: A physics class runs a computer simulation of the gold foil experiment. The program fires exactly 80,000 alpha particles at a thin gold foil and sorts them by how far each one is turned from its original path. The results are in the table below. Simulated alpha particles sorted by deflection angle Deflection angle Number of alpha particles 0° to 2° (almost straight through) 79,200 2° to 10° 790 10° to 90° 8 More than 90° (bounced back) 2 (a) What percent of the alpha particles went almost straight through? (b) What fraction were turned by more than 10°? Write it as "1 in ____." (c) Which rows would the plum pudding model predict to be zero? (d) What do the first and last rows each tell you about the atom?
hints.answer: (a) \( \dfrac{79{,}200}{80{,}000} \times 100\% = 99.0\% \) (b) 8 + 2 = 10 particles were turned by more than 10°. \( \dfrac{10}{80{,}000} = \dfrac{1}{8000} \), so 1 in 8000 . (c) The last two rows (10° to 90°, and more than 90°). With positive charge and mass spread thinly through each atom, nothing would be concentrated enough to turn an alpha particle sharply. (d) The first row shows that an atom is mostly empty space : 99.0% of the particles met nothing that could turn them. The last row shows that a few particles hit something small, dense, and positive , the nucleus, which is heavy enough and charged enough to push an alpha particle straight back.
hints.hint: (a) Divide the first row by the 80,000 total and multiply by 100%. (b) Add the last two rows and divide by the total. (c) (d) What could thinly spread charge never do?

hints.title: Problem 2.37
hints.question: Complete the table below. Each row describes one atom or ion. Isotopes and isotope ions to complete (blanks marked ?) Symbol Z A Protons Neutrons Electrons Charge \( ^{66}_{30}\text{Zn} \) ? ? ? ? ? ? \( ^{34}_{16}\text{S}^{2-} \) ? ? ? ? ? ? ? 92 235 ? ? ? 0 ? ? ? 27 33 25 ? ? 35 ? ? 46 ? 1− ? ? 39 ? ? 18 1+
hints.answer: Use the three rules: protons = Z; neutrons = A − Z; electrons = protons − charge. \( ^{66}_{30}\text{Zn} \): Z = 30, A = 66, 30 protons, 66 − 30 = 36 neutrons, 30 electrons, charge 0. \( ^{34}_{16}\text{S}^{2-} \): Z = 16, A = 34, 16 protons, 34 − 16 = 18 neutrons, 16 + 2 = 18 electrons, charge 2−. Z = 92 is uranium: \( ^{235}_{92}\text{U} \) (uranium-235); 92 protons, 235 − 92 = 143 neutrons, 92 electrons. 27 protons is cobalt: Z = 27, A = 27 + 33 = 60, charge = 27 − 25 = 2+, so \( ^{60}_{27}\text{Co}^{2+} \). Z = 35 is bromine: 35 protons, A = 35 + 46 = 81, electrons = 35 + 1 = 36, so \( ^{81}_{35}\text{Br}^{-} \). Protons = electrons + charge = 18 + 1 = 19, so Z = 19, potassium; neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20, so \( ^{39}_{19}\text{K}^{+} \). Notice that the charge never enters the neutron count.
hints.hint: Use the three rules: protons = Z; neutrons = A − Z; electrons = protons − charge. Find each row's fingerprint (protons or symbol) first.

hints.title: Problem 2.13
hints.question: Four elements, oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen, make up about 96% of the mass of the human body. Calcium and phosphorus, the main elements of bone mineral, come next. For each of these six elements, give the symbol, the atomic number, and the number of electrons in a neutral atom. Which of the six has the most protons?
hints.answer: Read each atomic number from the periodic table; in a neutral atom, electrons = protons = Z. Oxygen, O : Z = 8, 8 electrons. Carbon, C : Z = 6, 6 electrons. Hydrogen, H : Z = 1, 1 electron. Nitrogen, N : Z = 7, 7 electrons. Calcium, Ca : Z = 20, 20 electrons. Phosphorus, P : Z = 15, 15 electrons. Calcium has the most protons (20). Notice that the four most abundant elements in the body by mass all have small atomic numbers.
hints.hint: Read each atomic number from the periodic table; in a neutral atom, electrons = protons = Z. Then compare the six Z values.

hints.title: Problem 2.54
hints.question: The periodic table lists 85.47 amu for rubidium, which has two natural isotopes, rubidium-85 and rubidium-87. Which statement is correct? A. Every rubidium atom has a mass of 85.47 amu. B. No single rubidium atom has a mass of 85.47 amu; the value is a weighted average of the masses of rubidium-85 and rubidium-87 atoms. C. 85.47 is the mass number of rubidium. D. Natural rubidium is half rubidium-85 and half rubidium-87.
hints.answer: B. Each atom is either rubidium-85 (about 84.91 amu) or rubidium-87 (about 86.91 amu). 85.47 describes the natural mixture, not any one atom. A is the most common misunderstanding: the average describes the mixture. C is wrong: a mass number counts protons plus neutrons, so it is always a whole number and belongs to one isotope. D would give an average near 86. The real average, 85.47, is much closer to 85, so rubidium-85 is the large majority (about 72%).
hints.hint: Is the periodic-table value the mass of one atom, or a weighted average of a mixture? A mass number is always a whole number.

hints.title: Problem 2.60
hints.question: When a sulfur atom gains two electrons, the particle that forms is A. a cation with a 2+ charge B. an anion with a 2− charge C. an anion with a 2+ charge D. sulfur-34, a heavier isotope of sulfur
hints.answer: B. Gaining two negative electrons gives 16 protons and 18 electrons: charge = 16 − 18 = 2−. A negative ion is an anion (onions make you cry: anions are the negative ones). The ion is S 2− , sulfide. A gets the sign backward. Cations (cats have paws: "paws-itive") form when electrons are lost . C mixes the two: an anion is always negative. D confuses electrons with neutrons. Electrons have almost no mass and do not change the mass number; adding neutrons makes an isotope.
hints.hint: Gaining negative electrons makes the charge negative: charge = protons − electrons. Onions make you cry: which ions are the negative ones?

hints.title: Problem 2.65
hints.question: Silicon, the element in computer chips and in the quartz of Sierra granite, has three natural isotopes. Silicon-28 (27.977 amu) is 92.23% of silicon atoms and silicon-29 (28.976 amu) is 4.68%. The rest is silicon-30 (29.974 amu). (a) What is the percent abundance of silicon-30? A. 3.09% B. 7.77% C. 96.91% D. 33.3% Then (b) calculate silicon's average atomic mass.
hints.answer: (a) A. The three percents must add to 100%: 100.00% − 92.23% − 4.68% = 3.09% . B subtracted only silicon-28 (100.00 − 92.23) and forgot silicon-29. C added the two given percents instead of subtracting them from 100%. D assumes the three isotopes are equally common; the problem says they are not. (b) Change each percent to a decimal and keep each product in parentheses on the calculator: \( (0.9223)(27.977) + (0.0468)(28.976) + (0.0309)(29.974) = 25.803 + 1.3561 + 0.92620 = 28.09\ \text{amu} \) The answer is 28.09 amu , rounded to the hundredths place (the last place known in the 1.36 and 25.80 terms). It is very close to 28 because silicon-28 is the large majority, and it matches the yellow-sheet value.
hints.hint: (a) The three percents must add to 100%: subtract both given values. (b) Change each percent to a decimal, multiply by its mass, and add all three.

hints.title: Problem 2.24
hints.question: Some private wells in the Central Valley draw groundwater with naturally high arsenic, which comes from minerals in the sediments. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency limit for arsenic in drinking water is 10 micrograms per liter (µg/L). A test of one well reports 14 µg/L. (a) Give arsenic's symbol, group, and period, and classify it as a metal, nonmetal, or metalloid. (b) Express the well result in milligrams per liter. (c) Is the well above or below the limit?
hints.answer: (a) Arsenic, As : group 15, period 4, a metalloid (on the staircase). (b) \( \dfrac{14\ \mu\text{g}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mg}}{1000\ \mu\text{g}} = 0.014\ \text{mg/L} \) The result is 0.014 mg/L (two significant figures, like 14). (c) Above. 14 µg/L is greater than 10 µg/L (0.010 mg/L). Comparing the values in the same unit avoids mistakes.
hints.hint: (a) Find arsenic on the table and check the staircase. (b) Use 1 mg = 1000 µg as a conversion factor. (c) Compare the two values in the same unit.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: Predict the ion formed by each metal and give its electron count: (a) zinc, (b) silver, (c) aluminum.
hints.answer: Walk down the steps. (a) Zn 2+ : 30 − 2 = 28 electrons. (b) Ag + : 47 − 1 = 46 electrons. (c) Al 3+ : 13 − 3 = 10 electrons.
hints.hint: Use "the steps" from this section for these three fixed-charge metals: start at aluminum and walk down. Then electrons = Z − charge.

hints.title: Problem 2.43
hints.question: In a famous 1952 experiment, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase asked whether a virus's DNA or its protein carries its genes into a bacterium. They grew one batch of virus with radioactive phosphorus-32 and another with radioactive sulfur-35. DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur, and the virus's protein contains sulfur but almost no phosphorus. (a) How many protons and neutrons are in phosphorus-32 and in sulfur-35? (b) Ordinary phosphorus is phosphorus-31. How many neutrons does it have? (c) Why could the virus build these isotopes into its DNA and protein as if they were ordinary phosphorus and sulfur? (d) The phosphorus-32 label, not the sulfur-35 label, ended up inside the bacteria. What did that show?
hints.answer: (a) Phosphorus-32: Z = 15, so 15 protons , 32 − 15 = 17 neutrons . Sulfur-35: Z = 16, so 16 protons , 35 − 16 = 19 neutrons . (b) 31 − 15 = 16 neutrons . (c) Isotopes of an element have the same protons and electrons, so they behave the same way chemically. The cell's chemistry cannot tell them apart; only the radiation reveals where they went. (d) DNA, not protein, entered the bacteria, so DNA carries the genetic information . Each isotope acted as a tag for one kind of molecule.
hints.hint: Z gives protons; neutrons = A − Z. For (c), what decides chemical behavior? For (d), which molecule (DNA or protein) carried the label that got inside?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: A sodium lamp gives off yellow light at 589 nm. What is the energy gap, in joules, between the two levels involved?
hints.answer: \( \Delta E = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s})(3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1})}{5.89 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}} = 3.37 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} \) Slightly larger than the 656 nm red gap, as a shorter wavelength should be.
hints.hint: The photon's energy equals the gap between the levels. Convert 589 nm to meters and use ΔE = hc/λ.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Write the configuration of the oxide ion, O 2− . Which noble gas is it isoelectronic with?
hints.answer: O is 1s 2 2s 2 2p 4 ; adding 2 electrons gives 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 , isoelectronic with neon.
hints.hint: Write oxygen's configuration, then add 2 electrons to the last subshell. Which noble gas has that many electrons?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Which is larger: (a) N or P; (b) Na or Cl; (c) Ca or Ca 2+ ?
hints.answer: (a) P (one more shell). (b) Na (same shell, smaller nuclear charge). (c) Ca (the ion has lost its 4s shell).
hints.hint: Atoms get bigger going down and to the left. For (c), a cation is smaller than its atom: which electrons did Ca lose?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hints.question: A student writes copper's configuration as [Ar] 4s 2 3d 9 . What is wrong, and what is the correct configuration? How many unpaired electrons does a copper atom have?
hints.answer: Copper is an exception: a filled 3d subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d. Correct: [Ar] 4s 1 3d 10 (18 + 1 + 10 = 29). The five 3d orbitals are all paired, so there is 1 unpaired electron, the one in 4s.
hints.hint: Never end a configuration in s<sup>2</sup>d<sup>9</sup>: copper is an exception. Which arrangement of 3d is extra stable? Then draw 4s and 3d and count single arrows.

hints.title: Problem 3.61
hints.question: Which configuration describes a magnesium atom in an excited state? A. [Ne] 3s 2 B. [Ne] 3s 1 3p 1 C. [Ne] 3s 3 D. [Ne] 3s 2 3p 1
hints.answer: B. It still has 10 + 2 = 12 electrons (magnesium), but one 3s electron has moved up to 3p. A is magnesium's ground state. C is impossible (an s subshell holds only 2). D has 13 electrons: that is the ground state of aluminum, not magnesium.
hints.hint: An excited state keeps magnesium's 12 electrons but moves one up. Check each choice's electron count and each subshell's capacity.

hints.title: Problem 3.39
hints.question: Explain each fact in one sentence. (a) Neon and argon almost never react. (b) Magnesium forms Mg 2+ rather than gaining six electrons. (c) Carbon usually shares electrons instead of forming an ion. (d) Na + has the same electron configuration as neon, but it is not neon.
hints.answer: (a) Their valence shells are already full (ns 2 np 6 , an octet), so they have nothing to gain by gaining, losing, or sharing electrons. (b) Magnesium is only 2 electrons past neon, so losing 2 reaches an octet far more easily than gaining 6 to reach argon. (c) With 4 valence electrons, carbon is halfway: it would have to lose 4 or gain 4 to reach an octet, so it shares electrons instead (Chapter 6). (d) Na + still has 11 protons, and the number of protons decides the element; neon has 10.
hints.hint: Use valence electrons and the octet rule each time. (c) Count carbon's steps to the nearest noble gas. (d) What defines an element: electrons or protons?

hints.title: Problem 3.42
hints.question: Which pair of ions are both isoelectronic with krypton? A. Rb + and Br − B. K + and Cl − C. Sr 2+ and Na + D. Se 2− and Ca 2+
hints.answer: A. Krypton has 36 electrons. Rb + : 37 − 1 = 36. Br − : 35 + 1 = 36. Both match. B: K + (18) and Cl − (18) are both isoelectronic with argon. C: Sr 2+ (38 − 2 = 36) matches krypton, but Na + (10) matches neon. D: Se 2− (34 + 2 = 36) matches krypton, but Ca 2+ (18) matches argon.
hints.hint: Krypton has 36 electrons. Find each ion's electron count (Z − charge); both ions in the pair must match.

hints.title: Problem 3.58
hints.question: A sodium streetlamp shows a bright yellow line at 589 nm. This line comes from electrons dropping back to sodium's ground state. (a) What is the energy gap, in joules, between the two levels that produce this line? (b) If white light passed through cool sodium vapor, would you expect a dark line at 589 nm? Explain.
hints.answer: (a) The photon carries exactly the energy of the gap. Convert 589 nm to 5.89 × 10 −7 m: \( \Delta E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s})(3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1})}{5.89 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}} = 3.37 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} \) (b) Yes. Cool sodium atoms sit in the ground state, and this line's gap starts at the ground state, so the atoms can absorb a 589 nm photon and jump up across the same gap. Sodium's absorption spectrum has a dark line at 589 nm. (Not every emission line shows up this way: a cool gas absorbs mainly the lines that start from the ground state.)
hints.hint: (a) The photon's energy equals the gap: convert 589 nm to meters and use ΔE = hc/λ. (b) Absorption and emission use the same gaps.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: Rank Li, Cs, and F in order of increasing ionization energy.
hints.answer: Cs < Li < F. Cs is farthest down group 1; F is farthest right in period 2.
hints.hint: Ionization energy is highest at the upper right and lowest at the lower left. Place each element on a tiny sketch of the table.

hints.title: Problem 3.13
hints.question: Many older street lights in Central Valley towns are sodium vapor lamps, which glow yellow-orange at 589 nm. (a) What is the energy of one 589 nm photon? (b) In one sentence, explain why a sodium lamp gives off nearly one color instead of a full rainbow.
hints.answer: (a) \( 589\ \text{nm} = 5.89 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m} \), and \( E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s})(3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1})}{5.89 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}} = 3.37 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} \) (b) Sodium's electrons can occupy only certain energy levels, so only certain energy drops are possible, and the strongest of them always gives a photon of the same energy, which is light of the same wavelength, 589 nm.
hints.hint: (a) Convert to meters and use E = hc/λ. (b) What does the Bohr model say about sodium's allowed energy levels?

hints.title: Problem 3.40
hints.question: Some lab reports and IV (intravenous) fluid labels give electrolytes in milliequivalents (mEq), a unit that counts charge: 1 mmol of an ion with a 2+ charge is 2 mEq, and 1 mmol of a 1+ ion is 1 mEq. A blood test reports K + 4.1 mmol/L, Ca 2+ 2.35 mmol/L, and Mg 2+ 0.85 mmol/L. (a) Convert each to mEq/L. (b) Where does each ion's charge come from?
hints.answer: (a) Multiply by the size of the charge. The 1 or 2 is an exact counting number, so it does not limit significant figures. K + : \( 4.1\ \text{mmol/L} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mEq}}{1\ \text{mmol}} = 4.1\ \text{mEq/L} \) Ca 2+ : \( 2.35\ \text{mmol/L} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mEq}}{1\ \text{mmol}} = 4.70\ \text{mEq/L} \) Mg 2+ : \( 0.85\ \text{mmol/L} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mEq}}{1\ \text{mmol}} = 1.7\ \text{mEq/L} \) (b) From the number of valence electrons each atom gives up to reach an octet: potassium (group 1) loses 1, and calcium and magnesium (group 2) each lose 2.
hints.hint: (a) Multiply each mmol/L value by the size of the ion's charge; the charge is an exact count. (b) Count each atom's valence electrons and its steps to an octet.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Write the full and noble-gas configurations of aluminum.
hints.answer: Al (13 electrons): 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 1 , or [Ne] 3s 2 3p 1 .
hints.hint: Al has 13 electrons. Fill subshells in diagonal-method order until the superscripts add to 13; for the shorthand, use the noble gas from the row above.

hints.title: Problem 4.57
hints.question: Without the green sheet, use the T43 pattern to give the formula and charge of (a) the arsenate ion and (b) the tellurate ion. Then write the formulas of (c) potassium arsenate and (d) aluminum tellurate.
hints.answer: (a) As is in the "4" (group 15): 4 O atoms and the group 15 charge, AsO 4 3− (it looks like phosphate, right above it). (b) Te is in the "4" (group 16): TeO 4 2− (like sulfate). (c) K + and AsO 4 3− : K 3 AsO 4 . One arsenate, so no parentheses. (d) Al 3+ and TeO 4 2− : Al 2 (TeO 4 ) 3 . Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 0.
hints.hint: Find As and Te in the 4 of T43: four O each, with the charge of the ion right above (phosphate, sulfate). Then balance with K<sup>+</sup> and with Al<sup>3+</sup>.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hints.question: Write the formulas of (a) calcium silicate; (b) potassium tellurate; (c) aluminum borate; (d) Pb 4+ with carbonate.
hints.answer: (a) CaSiO 3 (silicate is SiO 3 2− , like carbonate). (b) K 2 TeO 4 . (c) AlBO 3 (3+ and 3− combine 1 : 1, no parentheses). (d) Pb 2 (CO 3 ) 4 reduces to Pb(CO 3 ) 2 .
hints.hint: Use T43: Si and B sit in the T (3 O), Te in the 4 (4 O); compare with carbonate, borate, and sulfate. For (d), swap-drop, then reduce the subscripts.

hints.title: Problem 4.15
hints.question: A student writes these formulas. Which are correct? Fix the ones that are wrong. (a) magnesium oxide, MgO 2 ; (b) aluminum hydroxide, Al(OH) 3 ; (c) calcium chloride, CaCl; (d) barium nitrate, Ba(NO 3 ) 2 ; (e) sodium sulfate, NaSO 4 .
hints.answer: (a) Wrong. Mg 2+ and O 2− combine 1 : 1: MgO . MgO 2 would have 4− of charge against 2+. (b) Correct. (3+) + 3(1−) = 0. (c) Wrong. Ca 2+ needs two Cl − : CaCl 2 . (d) Correct. (2+) + 2(1−) = 0. (e) Wrong. Sulfate is 2−, so it needs two Na + : Na 2 SO 4 .
hints.hint: Write the ions with their charges for each and check whether the total charge is zero. Fix a wrong one by changing how many ions, never the ion itself.

hints.title: Problem 4.28
hints.question: Write the formula of each compound: (a) carbon tetrabromide; (b) nitrogen dioxide; (c) xenon tetrafluoride; (d) diboron trioxide; (e) iodine monochloride; (f) tetrasulfur tetranitride.
hints.answer: (a) CBr 4 . (b) NO 2 . (c) XeF 4 . (d) B 2 O 3 . (e) ICl . (f) S 4 N 4 . The prefixes give the subscripts directly; there are no charges to balance, and S 4 N 4 is not reduced to SN.
hints.hint: Each prefix is a subscript: mono- = 1, di- = 2, tri- = 3, tetra- = 4. There are no charges to balance, and a molecular formula is never reduced.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Name (a) ZnBr 2 ; (b) Cu 2 S; (c) Fe(NO 3 ) 2 ; (d) (NH 4 ) 3 PO 4 .
hints.answer: (a) zinc bromide (no numeral: Zn is fixed at 2+). (b) copper(I) sulfide: one S 2− shared by two Cu, so each is 1+. (c) iron(II) nitrate: 2 NO 3 − = 2−. (d) ammonium phosphate.
hints.hint: First ask: is the metal on the fixed-charge list (group 1, group 2, Al, Zn, Ag)? If not, find its charge from the total anion charge and write it as a Roman numeral.

hints.title: Problem 4.40
hints.question: (a) Vinegar contains acetic acid. Write the formulas of acetic acid and of the acetate ion. Acetic acid has 4 H atoms in all; why is only one of them written in front? (b) Spinach contains oxalic acid, and calcium oxalate is the most common compound in kidney stones. Write the formulas of oxalic acid and calcium oxalate, and count the atoms in one formula unit of calcium oxalate.
hints.answer: (a) Acetic acid is HC 2 H 3 O 2 (also written CH 3 COOH), and acetate is C 2 H 3 O 2 − . Only the H written in front is released as H + ; the other 3 H atoms are part of the acetate ion. Acetate has a 1− charge, so the acid has one H + . (b) Oxalate is C 2 O 4 2− , so oxalic acid is H 2 C 2 O 4 and calcium oxalate (Ca 2+ with C 2 O 4 2− ) is CaC 2 O 4 : Ca 1, C 2, O 4, 7 atoms .
hints.hint: (a) Which H is written in front, and what is the acetate ion's charge? (b) Oxalate is 2− on the green sheet; balance it with H<sup>+</sup> or with Ca<sup>2+</sup>.

hints.title: Problem 4.36
hints.question: Write the formula of each acid: (a) hydrochloric acid; (b) phosphoric acid; (c) carbonic acid; (d) hypobromous acid; (e) oxalic acid; (f) iodic acid.
hints.answer: (a) hydro-...-ic from chloride, Cl − : HCl(aq) . (b) -ic from phosphate, PO 4 3− ; three H + cancel 3−: H 3 PO 4 . (c) -ic from carbonate, CO 3 2− : H 2 CO 3 . (d) hypo-...-ous from hypobromite, BrO − : HBrO . (e) from oxalate, C 2 O 4 2− : H 2 C 2 O 4 . (f) -ic from iodate, IO 3 − : HIO 3 .
hints.hint: Work backward to the anion: hydro-...-ic from -ide, -ic from -ate, -ous from -ite (keep hypo-). Then add one H<sup>+</sup> per negative charge.

hints.title: Problem 4.52
hints.question: Iron (Z = 26) forms the ions in ferrous sulfate, an iron supplement, and in ferric chloride. (a) How many protons and electrons are in Fe 2+ and in Fe 3+ ? (b) Write the formulas of iron(II) oxide and iron(III) oxide. (c) Which iron ion is in ferrous sulfate?
hints.answer: (a) Both have 26 protons , because the proton count identifies iron. Fe 2+ has 26 − 2 = 24 electrons ; Fe 3+ has 26 − 3 = 23 electrons . (b) Fe 2+ and O 2− : FeO . Fe 3+ and O 2− : Fe 2 O 3 . (c) Fe 2+ : ferrous is the lower charge (FeSO 4 , iron(II) sulfate).
hints.hint: (a) Protons = Z; a 2+ or 3+ ion has lost 2 or 3 electrons. (b) Swap-drop each iron ion with O<sup>2−</sup>. (c) -ous is the lower charge.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Name (a) HF(aq); (b) H 2 CO 3 ; (c) HClO 2 ; (d) HNO 3 .
hints.answer: (a) hydrofluoric acid. (b) carbonic acid. (c) chlorous acid (chlorite → -ous). (d) nitric acid.
hints.hint: Go through the anion: name the ion hiding after the H. An -ide ion gives hydro-...-ic acid, -ate gives -ic acid, and -ite gives -ous acid.

hints.title: Problem 4.63
hints.question: A bottle in the stockroom is labeled MnSO 4 . What is its correct name? A. magnesium sulfate B. manganese sulfate C. manganese(II) sulfate D. magnesium(II) sulfate
hints.answer: C. Mn is manganese, a transition metal that forms more than one ion, so it needs a Roman numeral. Sulfate is 2−, so the manganese is 2+: manganese(II) sulfate. A and D name the wrong metal. Magnesium is Mg (MgSO 4 , the electrolyte Mateo received by IV (intravenously)), and as a group 2 metal it never takes a numeral, so D is wrong twice. B is the right metal, but leaving off the numeral does not say which manganese ion is present.
hints.hint: Mn or Mg? Check the symbol on the periodic table. Then ask whether that metal has a fixed charge or needs a Roman numeral.

hints.title: Problem 4.19
hints.question: Give the Stock name (with a Roman numeral) and the older -ous/-ic name of each compound: (a) Fe(OH) 3 ; (b) CuCl; (c) Cr 2 O 3 ; (d) Pb(NO 3 ) 2 ; (e) Co(NO 3 ) 3 ; (f) SnCl 4 .
hints.answer: (a) 3 OH − = 3−, so Fe 3+ : iron(III) hydroxide , ferric hydroxide. (b) 1 Cl − , so Cu + : copper(I) chloride , cuprous chloride. (c) 3 O 2− = 6− over 2 Cr, so Cr 3+ : chromium(III) oxide , chromic oxide. (d) 2 NO 3 − = 2−, so Pb 2+ : lead(II) nitrate , plumbous nitrate. (e) 3 NO 3 − = 3−, so Co 3+ : cobalt(III) nitrate , cobaltic nitrate. (f) 4 Cl − = 4−, so Sn 4+ : tin(IV) chloride , stannic chloride. The -ous name always goes with the lower of the metal's two charges and -ic with the higher.
hints.hint: Find each metal's charge from the anions and write it as a Roman numeral. For the older name, use the Latin root with -ous for the lower charge, -ic for the higher.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Which of these elements are diatomic when uncombined: neon, nitrogen, sodium, bromine?
hints.answer: Nitrogen (N 2 ) and bromine (Br 2 ). Neon is a single-atom noble gas, and sodium is a metal.
hints.hint: Recall the seven diatomic elements: hydrogen plus the "7" shape that starts at nitrogen (N, O, F, then down the halogens). Which of these four are on that list?

hints.title: Problem 5.37
hints.question: What is the mass of 0.150 mol of carbon dioxide, CO 2 (44.009 g/mol)? A. 3.41 × 10 −3 g B. 6.60 g C. 293 g D. 9.03 × 10 22 g
hints.answer: B. Moles to grams: multiply by the molar mass. \( 0.150\ \text{mol CO}_2 \times \dfrac{44.009\ \text{g CO}_2}{1\ \text{mol CO}_2} = 6.60\ \text{g CO}_2 \) A divides moles by molar mass (0.150 ÷ 44.009); the units come out mol 2 /g, not g. C divides molar mass by moles (44.009 ÷ 0.150). Less than one mole must weigh less than 44 g, not more. D multiplies by Avogadro's number. That gives the number of molecules (9.03 × 10 22 ), not a mass in grams.
hints.hint: Moles to grams: which way does the molar mass factor go so moles cancel? Less than a mole should weigh less than the molar mass.

hints.title: Problem 5.29
hints.question: A total serum calcium result is 9.4 mg/dL. Convert it to mmol/L. (Ca 40.08; 1 L = 10 dL)
hints.answer: \( \dfrac{9.4\ \text{mg Ca}}{1\ \text{dL}} \times \dfrac{10\ \text{dL}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mmol Ca}}{40.08\ \text{mg Ca}} = 2.3\ \text{mmol/L} \) The result is 2.3 mmol/L , two significant figures like 9.4 (the 10 dL per L is exact). The "divide by 18" shortcut works only for glucose; every substance needs its own molar mass.
hints.hint: Same setup as the glucose problem, but with calcium's molar mass: dL to L, then mg to mmol (mg on the bottom).

hints.title: Problem 5.55
hints.question: Mateo's IV bag (chapter opener) contained 2.00 g of magnesium sulfate. (a) Write the formula of magnesium sulfate. (b) How many Mg 2+ ions does the bag contain? (c) What mass of magnesium, in mg, is that? (d) How many ions in total are released when it dissolves? (O 15.999, Mg 24.31, S 32.06)
hints.answer: (a) Mg 2+ and SO 4 2− combine 1 : 1: MgSO 4 , molar mass 24.31 + 32.06 + 4(15.999) = 120.37 g/mol. (b) \( 2.00\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol MgSO}_4}{120.37\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Mg}^{2+}}{1\ \text{mol MgSO}_4} \times \dfrac{6.0221 \times 10^{23}\ \text{ions}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 1.00 \times 10^{22}\ \text{Mg}^{2+}\ \text{ions} \) (c) \( 0.01662\ \text{mol Mg}^{2+} \times \dfrac{24.31\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mg}}{1\ \text{g}} = 404\ \text{mg Mg} \) (d) Each formula unit gives 2 ions (one Mg 2+ , one SO 4 2− ): 2 × 1.00 × 10 22 = 2.00 × 10 22 ions (0.0332 mol, as in Section 5.4). (b) 1.00 × 10 22 Mg 2+ ions ; (c) 404 mg of magnesium, about one-fifth of the 2.00 g salt mass. (Context only; this is not dosing guidance.)
hints.hint: (a) Balance Mg<sup>2+</sup> with sulfate. (b) Grams to moles, then Mg<sup>2+</sup> (1 : 1), then ions. (c) Moles of Mg to grams to mg. (d) How many ions per formula unit?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: A 0.155 mol sample of a metal used in jewelry has a mass of 30.5 g. Identify the metal.
hints.answer: 30.5 g ÷ 0.155 mol = 197 g/mol, which matches gold (196.97). Platinum (195.08) is close but further away.
hints.hint: Molar mass is grams per mole. Divide the mass by the moles, then find the jewelry metal whose atomic mass on the yellow sheet is closest.

hints.title: Problem 5.27
hints.question: An ibuprofen tablet contains 200. mg of ibuprofen, C 13 H 18 O 2 (206.285 g/mol). How many millimoles of ibuprofen is that? A. 0.970 mmol B. 970. mmol C. 4.13 × 10 4 mmol D. 9.70 × 10 −4 mmol
hints.answer: A. Because 1 mmol of ibuprofen has a mass of 206.285 mg (both units are scaled by 10 −3 ), the molar mass can be used as 206.285 mg/mmol: \( 200.\ \text{mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mmol}}{206.285\ \text{mg}} = 0.970\ \text{mmol} \) (The decimal point in "200." makes all three digits significant.) The same answer comes from 0.200 g ÷ 206.285 g/mol = 9.70 × 10 −4 mol = 0.970 mmol. B is a mg/g slip: it treats 200. mg as 200. g, which gives 0.970 mol , or 970. mmol, a thousand times too much. C multiplies by the molar mass instead of dividing; the units would be mg 2 /mmol, not mmol. D is the answer in moles (9.70 × 10 −4 mol) mislabeled as millimoles, or divided by 1000 one time too many.
hints.hint: Molar mass in g/mol is the same number in mg/mmol, so divide the mg by it directly. Should the answer be more or less than 1 mmol?

hints.title: Problem 5.58
hints.question: Bromine is a dark red liquid made of Br 2 molecules. How many bromine atoms are in 4.00 g of Br 2 ? (Br 79.90) A. 1.51 × 10 22 B. 3.01 × 10 22 C. 6.03 × 10 22 D. 7.70 × 10 26
hints.answer: B. Br 2 is 2(79.90) = 159.80 g/mol, and each molecule holds 2 atoms: \( 4.00\ \text{g Br}_2 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Br}_2}{159.80\ \text{g Br}_2} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol Br}}{1\ \text{mol Br}_2} \times \dfrac{6.0221 \times 10^{23}\ \text{Br atoms}}{1\ \text{mol Br}} = 3.01 \times 10^{22}\ \text{Br atoms} \) You get the same answer by using the atom's molar mass (79.90 g/mol) and no ×2 step, because 4.00 g of bromine is the same atoms either way. A is the number of Br 2 molecules : the ×2 step was skipped. C used 79.90 g/mol and multiplied by 2, counting every atom twice. D multiplied by the molar mass instead of dividing.
hints.hint: Bromine is diatomic: grams to moles of Br<sub>2</sub> (molar mass 2 × 79.90), then moles of Br atoms (2 per molecule), then atoms.

hints.title: Problem 5.43
hints.question: A CT contrast agent labeled "300" contains 647 mg of iohexol, C 19 H 26 I 3 N 3 O 9 (821.13 g/mol; Section 5.2), in each milliliter. (a) How many millimoles of iohexol are in 1 mL? (b) How many millimoles of iodine atoms? (c) What mass of iodine is in 1 mL? (I 126.90) (d) What does the "300" on the label mean?
hints.answer: (a) \( 647\ \text{mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mmol iohexol}}{821.13\ \text{mg}} = 0.788\ \text{mmol iohexol} \) (b) \( 0.7879\ \text{mmol iohexol} \times \dfrac{3\ \text{mmol I}}{1\ \text{mmol iohexol}} = 2.36\ \text{mmol I} \) (c) \( 2.364\ \text{mmol I} \times \dfrac{126.90\ \text{mg I}}{1\ \text{mmol I}} = 3.00 \times 10^{2}\ \text{mg I} \) (c) 300. mg of iodine (three significant figures, set by 647 mg). (d) The "300" is the iodine content, 300 mg of iodine per mL, not the iohexol content. Radiologic technologists read contrast strength as iodine, because the iodine atoms are what absorb the X-rays. Using 1 I per molecule instead of 3 gives 100. mg, a third of the true value.
hints.hint: (a) Divide mg by the molar mass as mg/mmol. (b) How many I atoms are in one iohexol formula? (c) Use iodine's molar mass. (d) Compare (c) with the label.

hints.title: Problem 5.60
hints.question: Bone mineral is mostly calcium phosphate, Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 . For 0.0150 mol of Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 , find (a) the moles of Ca 2+ ions, (b) the moles of PO 4 3− ions, (c) the total moles of ions, and (d) the moles of O atoms.
hints.answer: Read the ratios from the formula: per mole, 3 mol Ca 2+ , 2 mol PO 4 3− , and 2 × 4 = 8 mol O. (a) 0.0150 × 3 = 0.0450 mol Ca 2+ ; (b) 0.0150 × 2 = 0.0300 mol PO 4 3− ; (c) 0.0450 + 0.0300 = 0.0750 mol of ions (5 ions per formula unit); (d) 0.0150 × 8 = 0.120 mol O . Note that (b) and (d) are different: a phosphate ion is one particle that contains four O atoms.
hints.hint: Read the ratios from the formula: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup> per formula unit, and O atoms (4 in each phosphate). Ions and O atoms are different questions.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: How many atoms are in 0.250 mol of iron?
hints.answer: 0.250 mol × 6.0221 × 10 23 atoms/mol = 1.51 × 10 23 Fe atoms.
hints.hint: Given: moles of Fe. Desire: Fe atoms. Equality: 1 mol = Avogadro's number of atoms. Write the factor with mol on the bottom so moles cancel.

hints.title: Problem 5.33
hints.question: You have 10.0 g of each of the four substances below. Which sample contains the greatest number of molecules? A. water, H 2 O (18.015 g/mol) B. carbon dioxide, CO 2 (44.009 g/mol) C. methane, CH 4 (16.043 g/mol) D. All four contain the same number of molecules.
hints.answer: C. For the same mass, the substance with the smallest molar mass has the most moles, and so the most molecules: 10.0 g ÷ 16.043 g/mol = 0.623 mol CH 4 , or 3.75 × 10 23 molecules. (Water: 0.555 mol, 3.34 × 10 23 ; CO 2 : 0.227 mol, 1.37 × 10 23 .) A is close but second: water's molar mass (18.015) is a little larger than methane's (16.043), so 10.0 g of water is slightly fewer moles. B has it backward. Heavier molecules mean fewer of them fit into 10.0 g, so CO 2 has the fewest. D confuses equal masses with equal moles. Equal moles would have equal numbers of molecules; equal masses do not.
hints.hint: Same mass for each: does a smaller or a larger molar mass give more moles, and so more molecules?

hints.title: Problem 5.12
hints.question: A balloon holds 0.20 mol of helium atoms. Which answer reports the number of helium atoms with the correct significant figures? A. 1.2044 × 10 23 atoms B. 1.20 × 10 23 atoms C. 1.2 × 10 23 atoms D. 1 × 10 23 atoms
hints.answer: C. In multiplication, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures of the measured values. 0.20 has 2 significant figures (the trailing zero after the decimal point counts), and Avogadro's number as given has 5, so the answer has 2: 0.20 × 6.0221 × 10 23 = 1.2 × 10 23 . A copies every digit from the calculator (5 significant figures), more precision than 0.20 mol supports. B has 3 significant figures; it would be right for 0.200 mol. D has only 1 significant figure; it treats 0.20 as if it were 0.2.
hints.hint: In multiplication, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures. How many does the mole value have? (A trailing zero after the decimal point counts.)

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: How many moles of phosphate ions, and how many moles of oxygen atoms, are in 0.0250 mol of Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 ?
hints.answer: 0.0250 × 2 = 0.0500 mol PO 4 3− ; 0.0250 × 8 = 0.200 mol O atoms.
hints.hint: Decide whether each part asks about the ion or an element inside it. One formula unit has two phosphate ions, and each phosphate holds four O atoms.

hints.title: Problem 6.39
hints.question: A student analyzes a 5.00 g sample of pure sodium chloride from a grocery store and a 50.0 g sample of pure sodium chloride harvested from seawater. Which statement is true? (Na 22.99, Cl 35.45) A. Both samples are 39.34% sodium by mass. B. The 50.0 g sample has the greater percent sodium, because it is larger. C. The two samples have different percents, because they came from different sources. D. The 5.00 g sample is 39.34% sodium and the 50.0 g sample is 393.4% sodium.
hints.answer: A. By the law of constant composition, every sample of a pure compound has the same percent composition: 22.99 ÷ 58.44 × 100% = 39.34% Na , whatever the sample size or source. B confuses mass with percent. The larger sample contains more grams of sodium (19.7 g versus 1.97 g), but the same fraction of its mass is sodium. C: a pure compound has a fixed composition. Different sources can bring different impurities , but both samples here are pure NaCl. D multiplies the percent by the mass ratio. A percent can never exceed 100% for one part of a whole.
hints.hint: Think about the law of constant composition. Does the percent of an element in a pure compound depend on sample size or source?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: Copper(I) sulfide, Cu 2 S (159.16 g/mol), is a copper ore. What mass of copper is in 250. g of pure Cu 2 S? (Cu 63.55)
hints.answer: %Cu = 2(63.55) ÷ 159.16 × 100% = 79.86%. 250. g Cu 2 S × (79.86 g Cu / 100 g Cu 2 S) = 200. g Cu (3 significant figures; the decimal point in 250. makes the zero significant).
hints.hint: Find %Cu from the formula (two Cu per Cu<sub>2</sub>S), then use it as a conversion factor: g Cu per 100 g Cu<sub>2</sub>S.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Acetic acid has the empirical formula CH 2 O and a molar mass of 60.05 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?
hints.answer: CH 2 O = 30.026 g/mol; n = 60.05 ÷ 30.026 = 2.000; C 2 H 4 O 2 (written HC 2 H 3 O 2 in Section 4.5).
hints.hint: Find the empirical formula mass of CH<sub>2</sub>O, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. Multiply every subscript by n.

hints.title: Problem 6.35
hints.question: Which compound has the greatest percent oxygen by mass? (H 1.008, C 12.011, N 14.007, O 15.999) A. Carbon dioxide, CO 2 B. Water, H 2 O C. Hydrogen peroxide, H 2 O 2 D. Dinitrogen monoxide, N 2 O
hints.answer: C. H 2 O 2 : 2(15.999) ÷ 34.014 × 100% = 94.07% O . Its only other atoms are two very light H atoms. A: CO 2 is 2(15.999) ÷ 44.009 × 100% = 72.71% O. Having two O atoms does not guarantee the highest percent; the carbon atom adds 12 g/mol. B: H 2 O is 15.999 ÷ 18.015 × 100% = 88.81% O, high, but H 2 O 2 adds a second O with no extra H. D: N 2 O is 15.999 ÷ 44.013 × 100% = 36.35% O; the two N atoms make up most of the mass.
hints.hint: For each, find the mass of O in one mole and the molar mass, then part ÷ whole. More O atoms alone does not guarantee the highest percent.

hints.title: Problem 6.14
hints.question: Chloromethane, CH 3 Cl, has 14 valence electrons. Which description of its Lewis structure is correct? A. C in the center, single-bonded to three H atoms and to Cl; three lone pairs on Cl; no lone pairs on C B. Cl in the center, single-bonded to C and to the three H atoms; no lone pairs on Cl C. C in the center, single-bonded to three H atoms and to Cl; three lone pairs on Cl and one lone pair on C D. C in the center, single-bonded to three H atoms and double-bonded to Cl; two lone pairs on Cl
hints.answer: A. Carbon is central (H is never central, and halogens are usually on the outside). Four single bonds use 8 electrons; the other 6 go on Cl as three lone pairs. Check: C has 4 bonds (8 electrons), Cl has 1 bond + 3 lone pairs (8), each H has 2, and 8 + 6 = 14 electrons are used. B gives chlorine 4 bonds and carbon only 1. Chlorine usually forms 1 bond and carbon 4 (HONC), and carbon would have only 2 electrons. C uses 16 electrons, 2 more than the molecule has, and gives carbon 10 electrons, more than an octet. D uses 14 electrons, but carbon now has 5 bonds (10 electrons). Carbon never exceeds an octet, and chlorine usually forms only 1 bond.
hints.hint: Check each choice: total electrons used must be 14, carbon makes 4 bonds (HONC), Cl usually 1, and no atom other than H has more or less than 8.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: Which is the strongest bond: C–O, C=O, or C≡O?
hints.answer: C≡O, the triple bond (shortest and strongest), as in carbon monoxide.
hints.hint: Think about how many pairs are shared. The more shared pairs between two atoms, the shorter and stronger the bond.

hints.title: Problem 6.2
hints.question: The dull, protective coating that forms on aluminum irrigation pipe is aluminum oxide. Use electron-dot symbols to show how aluminum and oxygen atoms form this ionic compound. (a) How many valence electrons does each atom have? (b) How many Al and O atoms are needed so that electrons lost equal electrons gained? (c) What is the formula?
hints.answer: (a) Al (group 13) has 3 valence electrons (3 dots) and loses all three to form Al 3+ . O (group 16) has 6 valence electrons (6 dots) and gains 2 to form O 2− with an octet. (b) The smallest number that both 3 and 2 divide into is 6. Two Al atoms lose 2 × 3 = 6 electrons, and three O atoms gain 3 × 2 = 6 electrons: 2 Al (3 dots each) + 3 O (6 dots each) → 2 Al 3+ (no dots) + 3 O 2− (8 dots each) (c) Al 2 O 3 . Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 6+ − 6 = 0, the same formula swap-drop gives (Section 4.2).
hints.hint: (a) Use group numbers. (b) Find the smallest number both 3 (lost per Al) and 2 (gained per O) divide into. (c) Write the formula from those counts.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Why must the two oxygen atoms in O 2 share two pairs rather than one?
hints.answer: O 2 has 12 valence electrons. With a single bond (2 electrons) and the other 10 as lone pairs, one O can have an octet but the other has only 6 electrons. Sharing a second pair (a double bond, 4 electrons, plus 2 lone pairs on each O) gives both atoms 8 electrons and uses exactly 12.
hints.hint: Count O<sub>2</sub>'s valence electrons, then try a single bond. Does each O end up with 8 electrons using only that many?

hints.title: Problem 6.3
hints.question: The table below lists compounds you might find in a pharmacy, a dental office, or a Valley farm supply store. @media (max-width: 37.49em) { .mt-content-container .mt-responsive-table td[data-th] { padding-left: 9.5em !important; } } Classify each compound (blanks marked ?) Formula Name Everyday use Salt, base, metal oxide, or not ionic? CaO calcium oxide (quicklime) raising the pH of acidic soil ? Mg(OH) 2 magnesium hydroxide milk of magnesia (antacid) ? KNO 3 potassium nitrate fertilizer; toothpaste for sensitive teeth ? ZnO zinc oxide mineral sunscreen; diaper-rash cream ? (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 ammonium sulfate nitrogen and sulfur fertilizer ? N 2 O dinitrogen monoxide (nitrous oxide) sedation gas in dental offices ? Fill in the last column.
hints.answer: CaO: metal oxide (Ca 2+ and the oxide ion, O 2− ). With water it forms the base Ca(OH) 2 , which is why it raises soil pH. Mg(OH) 2 : base (a metal hydroxide; it contains OH − ). KNO 3 : salt (K + and the polyatomic nitrate ion; neither H + , OH − , nor O 2− ). ZnO: metal oxide (Zn 2+ and O 2− ). (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 : salt . It has no metal, but it is made of two kinds of ions, NH 4 + and SO 4 2− , so it is ionic. N 2 O: not ionic . Nitrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals, so N 2 O is a molecular (covalent) compound, named with prefixes (Section 4.4).
hints.hint: Look for the ions: OH<sup>−</sup> means base; a metal with O<sup>2−</sup> means metal oxide; other ion pairs (including NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) mean salt; two nonmetals with no ions means not ionic.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: What is the mass percent of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate, NH 4 NO 3 (80.043 g/mol)?
hints.answer: 2(14.007) ÷ 80.043 × 100% = 35.00% N. (Compare Section 5.4: the fertilizer grade 34-0-0.)
hints.hint: Mass of N in one mole: subscript × atomic mass (count every N in the formula). Then part ÷ whole × 100%.

hints.title: Problem 6.45
hints.question: Lactic acid builds up in muscles during intense exercise. Its empirical formula is CH 2 O and its molar mass is 90.08 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (H 1.008, C 12.011, O 15.999) A. CH 2 O B. C 2 H 4 O 2 C. C 3 H 6 O 3 D. C 6 H 12 O 6
hints.answer: C. The empirical formula mass is 12.011 + 2(1.008) + 15.999 = 30.026 g/mol, so \( n = \dfrac{90.08}{30.026} = 3.000 \) and the molecular formula is (CH 2 O) 3 = C 3 H 6 O 3 . A is the empirical formula. Its mass (30.03 g/mol) is only one-third of the given molar mass, so it cannot be the molecular formula. B uses n = 2 (60.05 g/mol, the molar mass of acetic acid, not lactic acid). D uses n = 6 (180.16 g/mol), the formula of glucose. Lactic acid is made from glucose in muscles, but each glucose gives two lactic acid molecules.
hints.hint: Find the empirical formula mass of CH<sub>2</sub>O, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. Which choice is (CH<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>n</sub>?

hints.title: Problem 6.36
hints.question: In Experiment 5a, a student records these masses: empty crucible and lid, 25.412 g; crucible, lid, and magnesium ribbon, 25.786 g; crucible, lid, and magnesium oxide after heating, 26.032 g. (a) Find the masses of magnesium, of product, and of oxygen that combined. (b) Find the percent Mg and percent O in the product. (c) Compare with the percent Mg in MgO, 60.31%.
hints.answer: (a) Mg: 25.786 − 25.412 = 0.374 g . Product: 26.032 − 25.412 = 0.620 g . Oxygen (conservation of mass): 0.620 − 0.374 = 0.246 g . (b) \( \%\text{Mg} = \dfrac{0.374\ \text{g}}{0.620\ \text{g}} \times 100\% = 60.3\% \qquad \%\text{O} = \dfrac{0.246\ \text{g}}{0.620\ \text{g}} \times 100\% = 39.7\% \) Three significant figures, set by the masses. Check: 60.3 + 39.7 = 100.0%. (c) 24.31 ÷ 40.31 × 100% = 60.31% Mg, so the student's 60.3% agrees with MgO within the precision of the data. Subtracting the crucible mass each time is the key step: the crucible is not part of the compound.
hints.hint: (a) Subtract the crucible mass each time; oxygen is product minus magnesium. (b) Part ÷ whole × 100%, where the whole is the product.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Balance the combustion of propane: C 3 H 8 (g) + O 2 (g) → CO 2 (g) + H 2 O(g).
hints.hint: Balance C, then H, then O. Count the O on the right after C and H; if it is even, divide by 2 for O<sub>2</sub>.

hints.title: Problem 7.17
hints.question: Almond shells and old orchard wood are mostly cellulose, whose repeating unit is C 6 H 10 O 5 . (a) Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of one C 6 H 10 O 5 unit. (b) When a pile of prunings smolders with too little air, what other products form besides CO 2 and H 2 O?
hints.answer: (a) C: 6 CO 2 . H: 10 H makes 5 H 2 O. O on the right: 6(2) + 5 = 17. The fuel already supplies 5 O, so O 2 must supply 17 − 5 = 12 O atoms, or 6 O 2 : C 6 H 10 O 5 (s) + 6 O 2 (g) → 6 CO 2 (g) + 5 H 2 O(g) Check: C 6 = 6; H 10 = 10; O 5 + 12 = 17 = 12 + 5. (b) Incomplete combustion also forms carbon monoxide (CO) and soot (carbon) , along with the fine particles (PM 2.5 ) that make smoke harmful to breathe. That is one reason open agricultural burning is restricted in the San Joaquin Valley.
hints.hint: (a) Balance C, then H, then O, and remember the fuel already supplies some O. (b) What does too little air do to the carbon products?

hints.title: Problem 7.33
hints.question: Predict the products and write each balanced equation with phase labels. (a) Sodium sulfide solution is mixed with hydrochloric acid, and a rotten-egg smell appears. (b) A grower mixes ammonium sulfate fertilizer with a slurry of lime, solid Ca(OH) 2 , and notices a sharp smell. Why do agronomists advise against applying ammonium fertilizers together with lime?
hints.answer: (a) Swap partners: Na + with Cl − (NaCl, soluble) and 2 H + with S 2− (H 2 S, already a gas): Na 2 S(aq) + 2 HCl(aq) → 2 NaCl(aq) + H 2 S(g) (b) Swap partners: Ca 2+ with SO 4 2− (CaSO 4 , insoluble sulfate exception) and NH 4 + with OH − (NH 4 OH, which is unstable). Replace each NH 4 OH with NH 3 (g) + H 2 O(l): (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 (aq) + Ca(OH) 2 (s) → CaSO 4 (s) + 2 NH 3 (g) + 2 H 2 O(l) Check: N 2 = 2; H 8 + 2 = 10 = 6 + 4; S 1 = 1; O 4 + 2 = 6 = 4 + 2; Ca 1 = 1. The sharp smell is ammonia gas. The nitrogen the crop needs escapes into the air as NH 3 , so mixing the two wastes fertilizer.
hints.hint: Swap partners. If you get H<sub>2</sub>S or NH<sub>4</sub>OH, check the unstable-products table: what does each really become? Watch the solubility of the calcium product.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Write the net ionic equation for mixing BaCl 2 (aq) and Na 2 SO 4 (aq).
hints.answer: Ba 2+ (aq) + SO 4 2− (aq) → BaSO 4 (s). Spectators: Na + , Cl − .
hints.hint: Swap partners and find the insoluble product with the green sheet. Write only the ions that build that solid.

hints.title: Problem 7.40
hints.question: Silverware and silver jewelry tarnish in air that contains traces of hydrogen sulfide: 4 Ag(s) + 2 H 2 S(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 Ag 2 S(s) + 2 H 2 O(l) Which substance is the oxidizing agent? A. Ag B. H 2 S C. O 2 D. Ag 2 S
hints.answer: C. Oxidation numbers: Ag 0 → +1 (in Ag 2 S, with S 2− ), so silver is oxidized. O 0 → −2 (in H 2 O), so oxygen is reduced. H stays +1 and S stays −2. The oxidizing agent is the reactant that contains the element reduced: O 2 . Check: 4 Ag each lose 1 electron (4 lost); 2 O atoms each gain 2 (4 gained). A: silver is oxidized, so Ag is the reducing agent. B: neither H (+1) nor S (−2) changes oxidation number, so H 2 S is neither oxidized nor reduced. D is a product. The oxidizing and reducing agents are reactants.
hints.hint: Assign oxidation numbers and find the element whose number decreases. The oxidizing agent is the reactant that contains it.

hints.title: Problem 7.45
hints.question: Use the activity series, listed from most active to least active: Li, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Sn, Pb, H 2 , Cu, Ag, Au Predict whether each reaction occurs. If it does, write the balanced equation; if not, write NR. (In these reactions, Fe, Sn, Ni, and Pb form 2+ ions.) (a) Fe(s) + Pb(NO 3 ) 2 (aq); (b) Ag(s) + Cu(NO 3 ) 2 (aq); (c) Al(s) + NiSO 4 (aq); (d) Sn(s) + HCl(aq); (e) Pb(s) + ZnCl 2 (aq).
hints.answer: (a) Fe is above Pb, so it reacts: Fe(s) + Pb(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) → Fe(NO 3 ) 2 (aq) + Pb(s) (b) Ag is below Cu: NR . (c) Al is above Ni, so it reacts. Al 3+ pairs with SO 4 2− as Al 2 (SO 4 ) 3 ; balance sulfate as a unit: 2 Al(s) + 3 NiSO 4 (aq) → Al 2 (SO 4 ) 3 (aq) + 3 Ni(s) (d) Sn is above H 2 , so it reacts (slowly) with the acid: Sn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → SnCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g) (e) Pb is below Zn: NR .
hints.hint: Compare the free metal with the metal ion (or H<sub>2</sub>) in the compound: a free metal displaces the ions of any metal below it. Balance any polyatomic ions as units.

hints.title: Problem 7.41
hints.question: Before digital imaging, X-ray departments recovered silver from used film-fixer solution by passing it through canisters of steel wool (iron). In simplified form, the reaction is iron metal reacting with silver ions to form iron(II) ions and silver metal. (a) Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions. (b) Combine them into the balanced net equation. (c) How many electrons are transferred?
hints.answer: (a) Oxidation (electrons on the right): Fe(s) → Fe 2+ (aq) + 2 e − Reduction (electrons on the left): Ag + (aq) + e − → Ag(s) (b) Iron loses 2 electrons but each Ag + gains only 1, so multiply the reduction by 2, add, and cancel the 2 e − : Fe(s) + 2 Ag + (aq) → Fe 2+ (aq) + 2 Ag(s) Check: charge 2(+1) = +2 on the left and +2 on the right. (c) 2 electrons .
hints.hint: (a) Iron loses electrons (written on the right); silver ions gain them (written on the left). (b) Multiply so the electrons match, then add and cancel.

hints.title: Problem 7.22
hints.question: All four compounds below matter in health care. According to the green-sheet solubility rules, which one is soluble in water? A. Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 , the mineral in bone B. CaC 2 O 4 , the main compound in most kidney stones C. BaSO 4 , the contrast agent swallowed before GI X-rays D. KCl, added to IV fluids to replace potassium
hints.answer: D. K + is a Group 1 ion, and every Group 1 compound is soluble. KCl dissolves completely into K + and Cl − , which is why it can be given in solution. A: phosphates are insoluble except with Group 1 and NH 4 + . Its insolubility is what lets calcium phosphate form hard, lasting bone. B: oxalate (C 2 O 4 2− ) is in the insoluble row, and Ca 2+ is not an exception, so calcium oxalate precipitates as stones. C: sulfate is usually soluble, but Ba 2+ is one of the exceptions. Because BaSO 4 barely dissolves, almost no toxic Ba 2+ is absorbed.
hints.hint: Check each against the green sheet. Which cation makes every compound soluble, and which anions have exceptions that include these cations?

hints.title: Problem 7.43
hints.question: Hydrogen peroxide whitens teeth and foams on a wound because it breaks down: 2 H 2 O 2 (aq) → 2 H 2 O(l) + O 2 (g) (a) Give the oxidation number of oxygen in H 2 O 2 , H 2 O, and O 2 . (b) Which oxygen atoms are oxidized and which are reduced? (c) What is unusual about the oxidizing and reducing agents here? (d) How many electrons are transferred in the equation as written?
hints.answer: (a) H 2 O 2 : H is +1, so 2(+1) + 2 O = 0 and O = −1 . H 2 O: O = −2 . O 2 : 0 (element). (b) The O atoms that end up in H 2 O go from −1 to −2: reduced . The O atoms that end up in O 2 go from −1 to 0: oxidized . (c) H 2 O 2 is both the oxidizing agent and the reducing agent. Some peroxide molecules give electrons to others. (d) The 2 O atoms in O 2 each lose 1 electron: 2 electrons . Check: the 2 O atoms in 2 H 2 O each gain 1 electron, 2 in all.
hints.hint: (a) Use the rule order: H is +1, so solve for O; an element is 0. (b) Follow each O atom to its product and see if its number goes up or down.

hints.title: Problem 7.13
hints.question: In the catalase test, a microbiology student mixes a bit of a bacterial colony with a drop of 3% hydrogen peroxide. The mixture bubbles right away. Which gas makes the bubbles, and what type of reaction is it? 2 H 2 O 2 (aq) → 2 H 2 O(l) + O 2 (g)    (catalase) A. CO 2 ; combustion B. O 2 ; decomposition C. H 2 ; single displacement D. O 2 ; combination
hints.answer: B. One reactant breaks down into two simpler products, so it is a decomposition, and the gas is oxygen, O 2 . The enzyme catalase is a catalyst, written over the arrow; bubbles mean the bacteria are catalase-positive. A: there is no carbon in the equation, so CO 2 cannot form, and combustion needs a fuel reacting with O 2 . Here O 2 is a product. C: no hydrogen gas forms, and a single displacement needs an element reacting with a compound. The only reactant is one compound. D has the right gas but the wrong pattern. A combination joins two or more reactants into one product; this is the reverse, one reactant into two products.
hints.hint: Read the equation: how many reactants and products are there, and which product is a gas? Match that to a pattern.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Classify: (a) 2 KClO 3 (s) → 2 KCl(s) + 3 O 2 (g); (b) Fe(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → FeCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g); (c) 4 Fe(s) + 3 O 2 (g) → 2 Fe 2 O 3 (s).
hints.answer: (a) decomposition. (b) single displacement. (c) combination (rusting).
hints.hint: Count reactants and products: one reactant breaking apart, an element replacing another, or elements joining into one product?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol, C 2 H 5 OH(l).
hints.hint: Supply CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. Balance C, then H, then O, remembering the fuel's own O atom.

hints.title: Problem 8.5
hints.question: Aluminum cookware is protected by a thin layer of aluminum oxide that forms in air: 4 Al(s) + 3 O 2 (g) → 2 Al 2 O 3 (s) For 0.600 mol of Al, find (a) the moles of O 2 that react and (b) the moles of Al 2 O 3 that form.
hints.answer: (a) \( 0.600\ \text{mol Al} \times \dfrac{3\ \text{mol O}_2}{4\ \text{mol Al}} = 0.450\ \text{mol O}_2 \) (b) \( 0.600\ \text{mol Al} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol Al}_2\text{O}_3}{4\ \text{mol Al}} = 0.300\ \text{mol Al}_2\text{O}_3 \) (a) 0.450 mol O 2 ; (b) 0.300 mol Al 2 O 3 . Check with the atoms: 0.300 mol Al 2 O 3 holds 0.600 mol Al, all of the aluminum you started with.
hints.hint: Use two mole ratios, each with 4 mol Al on the bottom: one to O<sub>2</sub> and one to Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

hints.title: Problem 8.13
hints.question: What mass of O 2 do your cells need to completely oxidize 15.0 g of glucose? Check your answer with conservation of mass. (C 6 H 12 O 6 180.156 g/mol; O 2 31.998 g/mol; CO 2 44.009 g/mol; H 2 O 18.015 g/mol) C 6 H 12 O 6 (aq) + 6 O 2 (g) → 6 CO 2 (g) + 6 H 2 O(l)
hints.answer: \( 15.0\ \text{g C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6}{180.156\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{6\ \text{mol O}_2}{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6} \times \dfrac{31.998\ \text{g O}_2}{1\ \text{mol O}_2} = 16.0\ \text{g O}_2 \) Your cells need 16.0 g of O 2 . Check: 0.08326 mol glucose makes 0.4996 mol each of CO 2 (22.0 g) and H 2 O (9.00 g). Reactants: 15.0 + 16.0 = 31.0 g. Products: 22.0 + 9.00 = 31.0 g. Mass is conserved.
hints.hint: Grams glucose → mol → mol O<sub>2</sub> (6 : 1) → grams O<sub>2</sub>. To check, find the masses of CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O too: reactant mass should equal product mass.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: For C 3 H 8 + 5 O 2 → 3 CO 2 + 4 H 2 O, how many moles of water form from 0.75 mol propane?
hints.answer: 0.75 × 4/1 = 3.0 mol H 2 O.
hints.hint: Find the coefficients of propane and water. Set up the mole ratio with mol H<sub>2</sub>O on top and mol C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> on the bottom.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: How many grams of O 2 are needed to burn 10.0 g of methane? CH 4 + 2 O 2 → CO 2 + 2 H 2 O (CH 4 16.043, O 2 31.998 g/mol)
hints.hint: Follow the road map: grams CH<sub>4</sub> → mol CH<sub>4</sub> → mol O<sub>2</sub> (mole ratio) → grams O<sub>2</sub>. The goal is the mole.

hints.title: Problem 8.15
hints.question: A student finds the mass of MgO made when 3.00 g of magnesium burns, 2 Mg(s) + O 2 (g) → 2 MgO(s), and writes \( 3.00\ \text{g Mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Mg}}{24.31\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol MgO}}{2\ \text{mol Mg}} \times \dfrac{2(40.31)\ \text{g MgO}}{1\ \text{mol MgO}} = 9.95\ \text{g MgO} \) (a) Find the mistake. (b) What is the correct mass? (c) How does conservation of mass show that 9.95 g is impossible? (Mg 24.31 g/mol; MgO 40.31 g/mol; O 2 31.998 g/mol)
hints.answer: (a) The student multiplied the molar mass by the coefficient. The coefficient 2 is already used in the mole ratio; the molar mass of MgO is 40.31 g/mol no matter what the equation says. (b) \( 3.00\ \text{g Mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Mg}}{24.31\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol MgO}}{2\ \text{mol Mg}} \times \dfrac{40.31\ \text{g MgO}}{1\ \text{mol MgO}} = 4.97\ \text{g MgO} \) (c) The O 2 used is 0.1234 mol Mg × (1/2) × 31.998 g/mol = 1.97 g, so the product can weigh only 3.00 + 1.97 = 4.97 g . To make 9.95 g, the magnesium would have to pick up 6.95 g of oxygen, more than three times what the equation allows.
hints.hint: (a) Look at the last factor: does a molar mass change with the coefficient? (c) The MgO mass must equal the Mg mass plus the O<sub>2</sub> used.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Write all six mole ratios for 2 H 2 O 2 → 2 H 2 O + O 2 .
hints.answer: 2 mol H 2 O 2 /2 mol H 2 O and its inverse; 2 mol H 2 O 2 /1 mol O 2 and its inverse; 2 mol H 2 O/1 mol O 2 and its inverse.
hints.hint: Three substances make three pairs. Each pair's coefficients give one ratio, and each ratio can be written either way up.

hints.title: Problem 8.30
hints.question: Iron filings are heated with powdered sulfur: Fe(s) + S(s) → FeS(s). A student uses 5.00 g of Fe and 3.50 g of S. Which reactant is limiting, and what mass of FeS can form? (Fe 55.85 g/mol; S 32.06 g/mol; FeS 87.91 g/mol) A. Fe is limiting; 7.87 g of FeS B. S is limiting; 9.60 g of FeS C. Fe is limiting; 9.60 g of FeS D. Neither is limiting; 8.50 g of FeS
hints.answer: A. FeS from each reactant (1 : 1 ratios): From Fe: 5.00 g ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 0.08953 mol Fe → 0.08953 mol FeS × 87.91 g/mol = 7.87 g From S: 3.50 g ÷ 32.06 g/mol = 0.1092 mol S → 0.1092 mol FeS × 87.91 g/mol = 9.60 g Fe makes less, so Fe is limiting and 7.87 g of FeS forms. Sulfur left: 3.50 − (0.08953 mol × 32.06 g/mol) = 3.50 − 2.87 = 0.63 g. B picks sulfur because it has the smaller mass. Mass is not moles: sulfur atoms are lighter, so 3.50 g of S is actually more moles than 5.00 g of Fe. C names the right limiting reactant but then calculates the product from the excess reactant. The product amount must come from the limiting reactant. D simply adds the two masses, assuming everything reacts. That is only true when the amounts match the recipe; here 0.63 g of sulfur is left over.
hints.hint: Convert both masses to moles (1 : 1 ratios), then to grams of FeS. The reactant that makes less FeS limits; a smaller mass does not mean fewer moles.

hints.title: Problem 8.31
hints.question: A 0.350 g piece of aluminum foil is dropped into a blue solution that contains 2.00 g of copper(II) chloride. Reddish copper metal forms as the blue color fades. 2 Al(s) + 3 CuCl 2 (aq) → 2 AlCl 3 (aq) + 3 Cu(s) (a) Which reactant is limiting? (b) What mass of Cu forms? (c) What mass of the excess reactant is left? (Al 26.98 g/mol; CuCl 2 134.45 g/mol; Cu 63.55 g/mol)
hints.answer: (a) Moles of Cu each reactant could make: From Al: 0.350 g ÷ 26.98 g/mol = 0.01297 mol Al × (3 mol Cu / 2 mol Al) = 0.01946 mol Cu From CuCl 2 : 2.00 g ÷ 134.45 g/mol = 0.01488 mol CuCl 2 × (3 mol Cu / 3 mol CuCl 2 ) = 0.01488 mol Cu CuCl 2 is limiting , so the blue color (from Cu 2+ ) disappears completely. (b) \( 0.01488\ \text{mol Cu} \times \dfrac{63.55\ \text{g Cu}}{1\ \text{mol Cu}} = 0.945\ \text{g Cu} \) (c) Al used: \( 0.01488\ \text{mol CuCl}_2 \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol Al}}{3\ \text{mol CuCl}_2} \times \dfrac{26.98\ \text{g Al}}{1\ \text{mol Al}} = 0.268\ \text{g Al} \) (b) 0.945 g Cu ; (c) Al left: 0.350 − 0.268 = 0.082 g Al (subtraction keeps three decimal places), a small piece of foil that stays shiny.
hints.hint: Find the moles of Cu each reactant could make (3 Cu : 2 Al; 3 Cu : 3 CuCl<sub>2</sub>). Then use the limiting reactant to find the Al used; excess = initial − used.

hints.title: Problem 8.52
hints.question: Ammonium sulfate, a fertilizer used on Valley orchards, is made from ammonia and sulfuric acid. A plant test run uses 34.0 g of NH 3 and 49.0 g of H 2 SO 4 and collects 61.5 g of product. (a) Write the formula of ammonium sulfate and the balanced equation (it is the only product). (b) Which reactant is limiting? (c) Find the theoretical yield and (d) the percent yield. (e) What mass of the excess reactant is left? (NH 3 17.031 g/mol; H 2 SO 4 98.07 g/mol; (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 132.13 g/mol)
hints.answer: (a) Two NH 4 + ions balance one SO 4 2− ion: (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 . Each NH 3 picks up one H + from the acid: 2 NH 3 (g) + H 2 SO 4 (aq) → (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 (aq) (b) Moles of (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 each reactant could make: From NH 3 : 34.0 g ÷ 17.031 g/mol = 1.996 mol × (1/2) = 0.9982 mol From H 2 SO 4 : 49.0 g ÷ 98.07 g/mol = 0.4996 mol × (1/1) = 0.4996 mol H 2 SO 4 is limiting , even though it has the larger mass. (c) \( 0.4996\ \text{mol} \times \dfrac{132.13\ \text{g (NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4}{1\ \text{mol}} = 66.0\ \text{g} \) (d) \( \dfrac{61.5\ \text{g}}{66.0\ \text{g}} \times 100\% = 93.2\% \) (e) NH 3 used: 0.4996 mol H 2 SO 4 × 2 = 0.9993 mol × 17.031 g/mol = 17.02 g. Left: 34.0 − 17.02 = 17.0 g NH 3 , half of what was loaded. (c) 66.0 g ; (d) 93.2% .
hints.hint: (a) Two NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> balance one SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>. (b) Find the moles of product each reactant could make; the bigger mass does not decide. (e) Excess = initial − used.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Is each exothermic or endothermic: (a) ΔH = +178 kJ; (b) a hand warmer heating up; (c) water evaporating from your skin?
hints.answer: (a) endothermic. (b) exothermic. (c) endothermic (it absorbs heat from your skin, which is why sweating cools you).
hints.hint: A positive ΔH means heat is absorbed. For (b) and (c), ask whether the surroundings (your hand, your skin) get warmer or colder.

hints.title: Problem 8.10
hints.question: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is flammable because ethanol burns: C 2 H 5 OH(l) + 3 O 2 (g) → 2 CO 2 (g) + 3 H 2 O(g) What mass of O 2 is needed to burn 5.00 g of ethanol? (C 2 H 5 OH 46.069 g/mol; O 2 31.998 g/mol) A. 10.4 g B. 3.47 g C. 1.16 g D. 31.3 g
hints.answer: A. \( 5.00\ \text{g C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}}{46.069\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{3\ \text{mol O}_2}{1\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}} \times \dfrac{31.998\ \text{g O}_2}{1\ \text{mol O}_2} = 10.4\ \text{g O}_2 \) B leaves out the mole ratio (0.1085 mol × 31.998 g/mol), as if 1 mol of ethanol used 1 mol of O 2 . C uses the flipped ratio, 1 mol ethanol / 3 mol O 2 . D multiplies the molar mass of O 2 by the coefficient (3 × 31.998 = 95.994 g/mol) and uses the 3 : 1 mole ratio, counting the 3 twice. The molar mass of O 2 is always 31.998 g/mol.
hints.hint: Set up grams → mol → mol → grams with the 3 : 1 mole ratio. Watch for choices that skip the ratio, flip it, or put a coefficient into a molar mass.

hints.title: Problem 8.4
hints.question: Yeast ferment glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide: C 6 H 12 O 6 (aq) → 2 C 2 H 5 OH(aq) + 2 CO 2 (g) How many moles of glucose must be fermented to make 3.40 mol of ethanol? A. 1.70 mol B. 6.80 mol C. 3.40 mol D. 0.567 mol
hints.answer: A. \( 3.40\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6}{2\ \text{mol C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}} = 1.70\ \text{mol C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \) Each glucose makes two ethanol molecules, so you need half as many moles of glucose as the ethanol you want. B uses the flipped ratio (2 mol glucose / 1 mol ethanol), which would need more glucose than ethanol made. C skips the mole ratio, as if 1 glucose made 1 ethanol. D divides by the subscript 6 in C 6 H 12 O 6 . Mole ratios between substances come from the coefficients, not from the subscripts inside a formula.
hints.hint: Work backward from the product: how many ethanol molecules does one glucose make? Should you need more or fewer moles of glucose than of ethanol?

hints.title: Problem 9.10
hints.question: After a dose of a fever reducer, a child's temperature drops by 2.5 °F. By how many degrees Celsius and by how many kelvins did it drop?
hints.answer: For a change in temperature, use only the size of the degrees; do not subtract 32 or add 273.15. A Celsius degree is 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, so \( \Delta T = \dfrac{2.5\ {}^\circ\text{F}}{1.8} = 1.4\ {}^\circ\text{C} = 1.4\ \text{K} \) The temperature dropped by 1.4 °C , which is also 1.4 K , because a kelvin is the same size as a Celsius degree. Using the full formula, (2.5 − 32)/1.8 = −16.4 °C, would convert a temperature of 2.5 °F, not a change. (Context only; this is not dosing guidance.)
hints.hint: This is a change in temperature, not a reading: do not subtract 32 or add 273.15. A Celsius degree is 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees; a kelvin is the same size as a Celsius degree.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
