hints.question: Liquid A has only weak dispersion forces; liquid B hydrogen bonds. Fill in "higher" or "lower" for liquid A compared with B: boiling point, vapor pressure, viscosity, surface tension.
hints.answer: Boiling point: lower. Vapor pressure: higher. Viscosity: lower. Surface tension: lower. (Vapor pressure is the one that goes the opposite way.)
hints.hint: Use the property table: weak forces give low values, except for the one row that runs the other way.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hints.question: Use the coin-flip model to explain why krypton (36 electrons) boils at a higher temperature than neon (10 electrons).
hints.answer: With 36 electrons, the chance of an exactly even split is only about 13%, versus about 25% for neon's 10. Krypton's electron cloud is lopsided more often (it is more polarizable), so it forms instantaneous dipoles more often, has stronger dispersion forces, and needs a higher temperature to boil.
hints.hint: Use the coin-flip table: is an exactly even split of electrons more or less likely with more electrons? What does a lopsided cloud do to dispersion forces?

hints.title: Problem 9.63
hints.question: A puddle of water and a puddle of rubbing alcohol are left on a sidewalk. (a) Using the spread of kinetic energies in a liquid, explain why both evaporate faster at 35 °C than at 15 °C. (b) Which puddle disappears first, and why? (c) Would spreading the water puddle thinner make it disappear faster or slower?
hints.answer: (a) Only molecules with more than the minimum kinetic energy needed to escape can evaporate. At 35 °C the distribution of kinetic energies shifts to higher values, so a larger fraction of molecules is above that minimum and evaporation is faster. (b) The rubbing alcohol . Isopropyl alcohol has only one O–H per molecule, so it forms fewer hydrogen bonds than water; its forces are weaker and its vapor pressure is higher (it is more volatile, and you can smell it). (c) Faster. A thinner, wider puddle has more surface area, so more molecules are at the surface in position to escape.
hints.hint: (a) Picture the hump of kinetic energies and the minimum energy needed to escape. (b) Which liquid forms fewer hydrogen bonds per molecule? (c) Where must a molecule be to escape?

hints.title: Problem 9.3
hints.question: A car brakes from highway speed to a stop. What happens to its kinetic energy? A. It is destroyed, because the car is no longer moving. B. It is turned back into chemical potential energy in the gasoline. C. It becomes temperature, which is a form of energy. D. It becomes heat in the brakes, tires, and air, so the total energy is unchanged.
hints.answer: D. By the law of conservation of energy, energy changes form but is never created or destroyed. Friction in the brakes turns the car's kinetic energy into heat, which is why brakes get hot after a hard stop. A breaks the law of conservation of energy. The car's kinetic energy is gone, but the energy itself has moved into the brakes and surroundings. B is backward. Burning gasoline is a one-way chemical change; ordinary brakes cannot rebuild fuel molecules. C confuses temperature with energy. The brakes' temperature rises because their particles gain kinetic energy, but temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, not a form of energy itself.
hints.hint: Energy changes form but is never created or destroyed. What gets hot when a car brakes hard? Temperature is a measurement, not a form of energy.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hints.question: How many joules are needed to warm 250. mL of water (density 1.00 g/mL) from 20.0 °C to 95.0 °C for a cup of tea?
hints.hint: Convert the volume to mass with the density first, then use q = mcΔT.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Classify each as exothermic or endothermic: (a) dew forming on grass; (b) a candle burning; (c) dry ice turning into gas.
hints.answer: (a) Exothermic (condensation releases heat). (b) Exothermic. (c) Endothermic (sublimation absorbs heat).
hints.hint: Ask whether the particles come together (heat released) or move apart (heat absorbed). Burning gives off heat and light.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Frozen vaccines are stored between −50.0 °C and −15.0 °C. Express this range in °F.
hints.answer: 1.8(−50.0) + 32 = −58.0 °F and 1.8(−15.0) + 32 = 5.0 °F, so −58.0 °F to 5.0 °F.
hints.hint: Use the yellow-sheet °C-to-°F formula on each end of the range: multiply first, then add 32. Keep the negative sign when you multiply.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Which of these can hydrogen bond with itself: CH 3 OH, CH 3 F, HF, H 2 , N(CH 3 ) 3 ?
hints.answer: CH 3 OH (O–H) and HF (H–F). CH 3 F and N(CH 3 ) 3 have H only on C; H 2 is nonpolar.
hints.hint: Look for an H bonded directly to N, O, or F. An H on carbon does not count.

hints.title: Problem 9.18
hints.question: A 455 g length of copper pipe cools from 65.0 °C to 22.5 °C. What is q for the pipe? A. +7.44 × 10 3 J B. −7.44 × 10 3 J C. −3.94 × 10 3 J D. −8.09 × 10 4 J
hints.answer: B. ΔT = T final − T initial = 22.5 − 65.0 = −42.5 °C. \( q = (455\ \text{g})\left(0.385\ \dfrac{\text{J}}{\text{g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C}}\right)(-42.5\ {}^\circ\text{C}) = -7.44 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J} \) The negative sign means the pipe releases 7.44 kJ of heat as it cools. A has the right size but the wrong sign; it comes from subtracting initial minus final. A cooling object releases heat, so q is negative. C uses the final temperature, 22.5 °C, as if it were ΔT. D uses the specific heat of water (4.184) instead of copper's (0.385). Use the specific heat of the substance whose temperature is changing.
hints.hint: Use q = mcΔT with c for copper, 0.385 J/(g·°C), and ΔT = final − initial. A cooling object releases heat, so what sign should q have?

hints.title: Problem 9.52
hints.question: A pot holding 1.20 × 10 3 g of soup (treat it as water) cools on the stove from 140.0 °F to 95.0 °F. (a) Convert both temperatures to °C. (b) Find q for the soup in kJ. (c) Express the heat released in food Calories. (d) Show that you get the same ΔT in °C by converting the change of 45.0 °F directly.
hints.answer: (a) \( \dfrac{140.0 - 32}{1.8} = \dfrac{108.0}{1.8} = 60.00\ {}^\circ\text{C} \qquad \dfrac{95.0 - 32}{1.8} = \dfrac{63.0}{1.8} = 35.0\ {}^\circ\text{C} \) (a) 60.00 °C (108.0 has four significant figures) and 35.0 °C . (b) \( q = (1.20 \times 10^{3}\ \text{g})(4.184)(35.0 - 60.00\ {}^\circ\text{C}) = (1.20 \times 10^{3})(4.184)(-25.0) = -1.26 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J} = -126\ \text{kJ} \) (b) q = −126 kJ ; the negative sign means the soup releases heat. The subtraction gives −25.0 (tenths place), and three significant figures limit the product. (c) 1.2552 × 10 5 J ÷ 4184 J/Cal = 30.0 Cal released. (d) ΔT = 45.0 °F ÷ 1.8 = 25.0 °C, the same size as 60.00 − 35.0. For a change, divide by 1.8 but do not subtract 32.
hints.hint: (a) °C = (°F − 32)/1.8. (b) q = mcΔT with ΔT = final − initial. (c) Divide kJ by 4.184 kJ/Cal. (d) For a change, just divide the °F change by 1.8.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: A white solid melts at 801 °C, does not conduct as a solid, and conducts when dissolved in water. What type of solid is it?
hints.answer: Ionic (it is NaCl).
hints.hint: Use the property clues: a high melting point, and conduction only when melted or dissolved. Which type of solid has charged particles locked in place?

hints.title: Problem 10.49
hints.question: Mateo Herrera, 34, is an irrigation technician on a Fresno County almond orchard. He has asthma and was admitted overnight on oxygen at 2.0 L/min by nasal cannula. The barometric pressure at the hospital is 757 mmHg. (a) Room air is 21.0% O 2 . What is the partial pressure of O 2 in dry room air? (b) His nose and airways warm the air to 37 °C and saturate it with water vapor (47.1 mmHg at 37 °C). What is the partial pressure of O 2 in this humidified air, still with 21.0% of the dry gas as O 2 ? (c) With the cannula, the oxygen fraction of the dry gas he inhales rises to about 0.280. Repeat (b). (d) The flowmeter measures the oxygen at room temperature, 21.0 °C. At constant pressure, what volume per minute does it fill once it warms to 37.0 °C in his airways?
hints.answer: (a) P O 2 = 0.210 × 757 mmHg = 159 mmHg . (b) The water vapor takes 47.1 mmHg of the total, leaving 757 − 47.1 = 709.9 mmHg for the dry gases, of which O 2 is 21.0%: \( P_{\text{O}_2} = 0.210 \times (757 - 47.1)\ \text{mmHg} = 0.210 \times 709.9\ \text{mmHg} = 149\ \text{mmHg} \) (c) 0.280 × 709.9 mmHg = 199 mmHg . (d) \( V_2 = V_1 \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 2.0\ \tfrac{\text{L}}{\text{min}} \times \dfrac{310.15\ \text{K}}{294.15\ \text{K}} = 2.1\ \tfrac{\text{L}}{\text{min}} \) (a) 159 mmHg ; (b) 149 mmHg ; (c) 199 mmHg ; (d) 2.1 L/min , two significant figures like 2.0 L/min. Raising the inspired PO 2 by about 50 mmHg pushes more oxygen across the alveolar walls by diffusion. (The case is for practicing chemistry only; oxygen is a medication and is given as ordered, and this is not treatment advice.)
hints.hint: (a) Mole fraction × pressure. (b) Subtract the water vapor first, then take the O<sub>2</sub> fraction of what is left. (c) Repeat with the new fraction. (d) Charles's law, in kelvins.

hints.title: Problem 10.24
hints.question: A small cartridge for inflating a bike tire holds 16.0 g of CO 2 (44.009 g/mol). What volume would this gas occupy at 1.00 atm and 20.0 °C?
hints.answer: Grams to moles first: n = 16.0 g ÷ 44.009 g/mol = 0.3636 mol. T = 293.15 K. \( V = \dfrac{nRT}{P} = \dfrac{(0.3636\ \text{mol})(0.082058)(293.15\ \text{K})}{1.00\ \text{atm}} = 8.75\ \text{L} \) The gas would fill 8.75 L at 1.00 atm. A road-bike tire holds only about 0.7 L, but at several atmospheres, so one cartridge fills one tire.
hints.hint: Our goal is the mole: change grams of CO<sub>2</sub> to moles first. Then V = nRT/P with T in kelvins.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: A mixture contains 1.50 mol N 2 and 0.500 mol CO 2 at a total pressure of 3.00 atm. What is the partial pressure of CO 2 ?
hints.hint: Find the mole fraction of CO<sub>2</sub> (its moles over the total moles), then multiply by the total pressure.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: A drawing of a gas sample shows 9 particles of gas A and 3 particles of gas B at a total pressure of 800. mmHg. What is the partial pressure of B?
hints.hint: Count particles: the mole fraction of B is its particles over all the particles. Multiply that fraction by the total pressure.

hints.title: Problem 10.6
hints.question: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas? A. High pressure and low temperature B. High pressure and high temperature C. Low pressure and high temperature D. Low pressure and low temperature
hints.answer: C. At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their own volume is a tiny fraction of the container. At high temperature they move so fast that attractions between them hardly matter. Both match the assumptions of kinetic molecular theory. A is the worst case: at high pressure the particles are crowded, and at low temperature attractions become important; this is how gases are liquefied, as with the liquid oxygen stored at hospitals. B fixes the temperature but not the crowding: at high pressure the particles' own volume still matters. D fixes the crowding but not the attractions: slow particles near the boiling point stick together.
hints.hint: An ideal gas has particles that take up no space and do not attract each other. Which pressure keeps particles far apart, and which temperature makes attractions unimportant?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: For 2 CO(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 CO 2 (g), what volume of O 2 is needed to burn 6.00 L of CO, both at the same temperature and pressure?
hints.answer: 6.00 L CO × (1 L O 2 / 2 L CO) = 3.00 L O 2 .
hints.hint: Both gases are at the same temperature and pressure, so the coefficients are volume ratios. Read the ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to CO from the equation.

hints.title: Problem 10.60
hints.question: A 0.562 g sample of a diatomic element occupies 0.520 L at 0.950 atm and 27.0 °C. Identify the element.
hints.answer: \( n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{(0.950)(0.520)}{(0.082058)(300.15)} = 0.02006\ \text{mol} \qquad M = \dfrac{0.562\ \text{g}}{0.02006\ \text{mol}} = 28.0\ \text{g/mol} \) Half of 28.0 is 14.0, the atomic mass of nitrogen. The gas is N 2 (28.014 g/mol). On the calculator, put (0.082058 × 300.15) in parentheses.
hints.hint: n = PV/RT (kelvins; parentheses around R × T), then M = grams ÷ moles. The element is diatomic, so halve the molar mass before checking the periodic table.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: What volume does 4.40 g of CO 2 occupy at STP?
hints.hint: Our goal is the mole: change grams to moles with the molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub>, then use 22.4 L/mol, which works because the gas is at STP.

hints.title: Problem 10.1
hints.question: Which statement is not part of kinetic molecular theory for an ideal gas? A. The particles are in constant, random, straight-line motion. B. The particles attract one another, which holds the gas together. C. Collisions between particles and with the walls are elastic. D. The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the Kelvin temperature.
hints.answer: B. Kinetic molecular theory assumes the particles neither attract nor repel each other. Nothing holds a gas together, which is why it spreads out to fill any container. (Attractions do matter for real gases near condensation, which is why the ideal model fails there.) A is part of the theory: constant random motion explains diffusion and why a gas fills its container. C is part of the theory: in elastic collisions no kinetic energy is lost overall, so a gas left alone at constant temperature never "runs down" and its pressure stays steady. D is part of the theory, and it is the reason every gas law needs temperatures in kelvins.
hints.hint: Compare each choice with the KMT list in Section 10.1. A gas spreads out to fill any container: what does that say about forces between its particles?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: A blood pressure reading is 118/76 mmHg. Express the systolic value, 118 mmHg, in atm.
hints.hint: Set up a conversion factor with 1 atm on top and 760 mmHg on the bottom so mmHg cancels.

hints.title: Problem 10.42
hints.question: In the Valley's summer smog, nitric oxide from vehicle exhaust reacts with oxygen to make brown nitrogen dioxide, which helps form ozone: 2 NO(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 NO 2 (g) In a lab model, 0.600 L of NO is mixed with 0.400 L of O 2 , all at the same temperature and pressure. (a) Which gas is limiting? (b) What volume of NO 2 forms? (c) What volume of the excess gas is left over? (d) What is the total volume of gas after the reaction, at the same T and P?
hints.answer: (a) To react completely, 0.600 L NO needs 0.600 × (1/2) = 0.300 L O 2 . There is 0.400 L, more than enough, so NO is limiting and O 2 is in excess. (b) 0.600 L NO × (2 L NO 2 / 2 L NO) = 0.600 L NO 2 . (c) 0.400 − 0.300 = 0.100 L O 2 left over. (d) 0.600 L NO 2 + 0.100 L O 2 = 0.700 L , less than the 1.000 L at the start, because 3 molecules of reactant gas become 2 molecules of product gas. All of these shortcuts work only because every gas is at the same T and P.
hints.hint: Same T and P, so work in liters with the coefficients. (a) Find how much O<sub>2</sub> the NO needs and compare with what is there. Use the limiting gas for the rest.

hints.title: Problem 10.13
hints.question: A student traps air in a sealed syringe attached to a pressure sensor, pushes the plunger in to several positions at constant temperature, and records the data in the table below. @media (max-width: 37.49em) { .mt-content-container .mt-responsive-table td[data-th] { padding-left: 9.5em !important; } } Pressure and volume of trapped air at constant temperature Trial Pressure (atm) Volume (mL) 1 1.00 24.0 2 1.50 16.0 3 2.00 12.0 4 3.00 8.00 (a) Is the relationship between P and V direct or inverse? Which gas law is this? (b) Show that one combination of P and V stays constant. (c) Predict the volume at 4.00 atm.
hints.answer: (a) As the pressure goes up, the volume goes down: doubling P from 1.00 to 2.00 atm halves V from 24.0 to 12.0 mL. This is an inverse relationship, Boyle's law . (b) The product PV is constant: (1.00)(24.0) = (1.50)(16.0) = (2.00)(12.0) = (3.00)(8.00) = 24.0 atm·mL in every trial. (The ratio V/P is not constant: 24.0, 10.7, 6.00, 2.67.) (c) \( V_2 = \dfrac{P_1 V_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{(1.00\ \text{atm})(24.0\ \text{mL})}{4.00\ \text{atm}} = 6.00\ \text{mL} \) (c) 6.00 mL , which continues the pattern: four times the pressure of trial 1, one-fourth the volume.
hints.hint: (a) As P goes up, what does V do? (b) Try both P × V and V/P for each trial; which stays the same? (c) Use P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.

hints.title: Problem 11.13
hints.question: At 0 °C, CO 2 dissolves in water to 3.35 g/L when the CO 2 pressure above the water is 1.00 atm. (a) A soda is bottled ice cold under a CO 2 pressure of 2.40 atm. How much CO 2 does each liter hold? (b) After the bottle is opened, the soda is in contact with air, where the CO 2 partial pressure is only about 4.0 × 10 −4 atm. How much CO 2 could a liter hold once it reaches equilibrium with the air at 0 °C? (c) An open soda takes hours to go completely flat, and a warm one goes flat faster. Explain both.
hints.answer: (a) \( S_2 = 3.35\ \tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{2.40\ \text{atm}}{1.00\ \text{atm}} = 8.04\ \tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{L}} \) (b) \( S_2 = 3.35\ \tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{atm}}{1.00\ \text{atm}} = 1.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{L}} \) (a) 8.04 g/L ; (b) 1.3 × 10 −3 g/L (two significant figures, set by 4.0 × 10 −4 atm), almost none. (c) Henry's law tells how much CO 2 the soda holds at equilibrium, not how fast it gets there. The extra CO 2 escapes only at the surface and as bubbles, which takes time. In a warm soda, CO 2 is less soluble to begin with and its faster molecules escape more quickly, so it goes flat sooner.
hints.hint: (a), (b) Henry's law: S<sub>2</sub> = S<sub>1</sub> × P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>. (c) Henry's law says how much stays dissolved, not how fast it leaves; how does warmth change both?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: The solubility of N 2 in blood at a partial pressure of 0.78 atm is S. What is its solubility when a diver is at a depth where the N 2 partial pressure is 2.34 atm?
hints.answer: S 2 = S × 2.34/0.78 = 3.0 S: three times as much N 2 dissolves.
hints.hint: Henry's law: S<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = S<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>2</sub> at constant temperature. By what factor did the N<sub>2</sub> partial pressure increase?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: What mass of AgCl (143.32 g/mol) precipitates when 30.0 mL of 0.250 M NaCl reacts with excess AgNO 3 ? NaCl + AgNO 3 → AgCl + NaNO 3
hints.answer: 0.0300 × 0.250 = 7.50 × 10 −3 mol AgCl; × 143.32 = 1.07 g.
hints.hint: Volume (in L) × molarity gives moles of NaCl; the ratio to AgCl is 1 : 1; then multiply by the molar mass of AgCl.

hints.title: Problem 11.26
hints.question: Mateo Herrera, 34, is an irrigation technician on a Fresno County almond orchard. He has asthma and was admitted overnight with an IV of 0.9% NaCl (normal saline); take it as 0.900% (m/v). His IV pump runs at 75.0 mL/h for 6.00 h. (a) What volume of saline does he receive? (b) How many grams of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) is that? (c) How many millimoles of NaCl, and so of Na + ions? (d) What is the molarity of 0.900% NaCl? Use it to check (c).
hints.answer: (a) 75.0 mL/h × 6.00 h = 450. mL (the decimal point shows three significant figures). (b) \( 450.\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{0.900\ \text{g NaCl}}{100\ \text{mL}} = 4.05\ \text{g NaCl} \) (c) \( 4.05\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{58.44\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mmol}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 69.3\ \text{mmol NaCl} \) Each NaCl gives one Na + , so that is also 69.3 mmol Na + . (d) 0.900 g per 100 mL is 9.00 g per liter: 9.00 g ÷ 58.44 g/mol = 0.154 M . Check: 0.450 L × 0.1540 mol/L = 0.0693 mol = 69.3 mmol. The answers: (a) 450. mL ; (b) 4.05 g ; (c) 69.3 mmol ; (d) 0.154 M . (The case is for practicing chemistry only; IV fluids are given exactly as ordered, and this is not treatment advice.)
hints.hint: (a) Rate × time. (b) Use 0.900 g per 100 mL as a conversion factor. (c) Grams to moles to mmol; how many Na<sup>+</sup> per NaCl? (d) Grams per liter ÷ molar mass.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: A sugar syrup is 15.0% sugar by mass. How many grams of syrup contain 30.0 g of sugar?
hints.answer: 30.0 g sugar × (100 g syrup / 15.0 g sugar) = 200. g syrup.
hints.hint: Start with the term by itself, the grams of sugar, and write the percent upside down (g syrup on top) so grams of sugar cancel.

hints.title: Problem 11.61
hints.question: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point? A. 0.20 m glucose B. 0.10 m Ca(C 2 H 3 O 2 ) 2 C. 0.12 m NaCl D. 0.080 m FeCl 3
hints.answer: D. Count particles, then multiply by molality: FeCl 3 → Fe 3+ + 3 Cl − , i = 4, and 4 × 0.080 = 0.32 m of particles, the most of the four. A: glucose stays whole (i = 1), so 0.20 m of particles. Its molality is the largest, but its particle count is the smallest. B: Ca(C 2 H 3 O 2 ) 2 gives Ca 2+ + 2 C 2 H 3 O 2 − , i = 3: 0.30 m, close but less than 0.32 m. C: NaCl gives 2 ions: 0.24 m.
hints.hint: Count particles: find i for each solute (acetate stays together) and multiply by its molality. The largest i × m freezes lowest.

hints.title: Problem 11.12
hints.question: At the surface, where the partial pressure of N 2 is 0.781 atm, a diver's blood holds about 12.5 mg of dissolved N 2 per liter (a round value for practice). (a) She descends to a depth where the air she breathes from her tank is at a total pressure of 3.20 atm and is 78.1% N 2 . What is the partial pressure of N 2 ? (b) Once her blood comes to equilibrium at that depth, how much N 2 is dissolved per liter? (c) Use Henry's law to explain why rising to the surface too quickly can cause decompression sickness.
hints.answer: (a) P N 2 = 0.781 × 3.20 atm = 2.50 atm (2.4992 atm unrounded). (b) \( S_2 = S_1 \times \dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = 12.5\ \tfrac{\text{mg}}{\text{L}} \times \dfrac{2.4992\ \text{atm}}{0.781\ \text{atm}} = 40.0\ \tfrac{\text{mg}}{\text{L}} \) (b) 40.0 mg/L , 3.20 times the surface value, because the N 2 pressure is 3.20 times higher. (c) As she rises, the N 2 pressure drops, so the blood can hold less N 2 . Rising slowly lets the extra gas leave through the lungs a little at a time. Rising fast is like opening a shaken soda: the gas comes out of solution as bubbles in the blood and tissues. (Context only; dive limits come from training agencies and dive computers.)
hints.hint: (a) Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure. (b) Henry's law, S<sub>1</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = S<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>2</sub>. (c) What happens to the solubility as the N<sub>2</sub> pressure drops?

hints.title: Problem 11.5
hints.question: The solubility of KCl is 34.2 g per 100 g of water at 20 °C. At 20 °C, a student stirs 17.1 g of KCl into 50.0 g of water, and all of it dissolves with nothing left over. How should the solution be classified? A. Unsaturated, because 17.1 g is less than 34.2 g B. Saturated C. Supersaturated D. It cannot be classified without the volume of the solution
hints.answer: B. The solubility is given per 100 g of water, but the student used only 50.0 g, half as much. Scale the amount dissolved to 100 g of water: \( \dfrac{17.1\ \text{g KCl}}{50.0\ \text{g water}} \times 100\ \text{g water} = 34.2\ \text{g KCl per 100 g water} \) That equals the solubility, so the solution holds the maximum: it is saturated. A compares 17.1 g with 34.2 g without matching the amounts of water. Half as much water holds only half as much KCl, 17.1 g. C would need more than 34.2 g per 100 g of water, held in solution by careful cooling. D is wrong because solubility tables are written per mass of water; the mass of water and the temperature are all you need.
hints.hint: Solubility is per 100 g of water, but only 50.0 g of water was used. Scale the amount dissolved to 100 g of water before comparing.

hints.title: Problem 11.57
hints.question: You need 300. mL of 0.250 M NaOH. The shelf has two bottles: 0.100 M NaOH and 2.00 M NaOH. (a) Which bottle can you use, and why? (b) What volume of it do you need? (c) How do you make the solution?
hints.answer: (a) The 2.00 M bottle. Dilution only lowers a concentration, and 0.100 M is already weaker than 0.250 M, so it can never become 0.250 M by adding water. (b) \( V_1 = \dfrac{M_2 V_2}{M_1} = \dfrac{(0.250\ M)(300.\ \text{mL})}{2.00\ M} = 37.5\ \text{mL} \) (c) Measure 37.5 mL of the 2.00 M stock into a container marked at 300. mL (a volumetric flask if one is available) and add deionized water up to the 300. mL mark, then mix. Do not measure 262.5 mL of water separately; filling to the mark gives the right total volume.
hints.hint: (a) Dilution only lowers a concentration: which bottle is stronger than the target? (b) M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. (c) Fill to the mark rather than measuring the water.

hints.title: Problem 11.24
hints.question: What mass of KCl (74.55 g/mol) is in 40.0 mL of 0.275 M KCl? A. 0.820 g B. 820. g C. 0.0110 g D. 10.8 g
hints.answer: A. \( 0.0400\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{0.275\ \text{mol KCl}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{74.55\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 0.820\ \text{g KCl} \) B multiplies by 40.0 mL without converting to liters, so the answer is 1000 times too large. C stops at moles (0.0110 mol) and labels them grams. D divides the volume by the molarity (0.0400 ÷ 0.275) instead of multiplying. Molarity times liters gives moles.
hints.hint: Change mL to L, multiply by the molarity to get moles, then multiply by the molar mass to get grams.

hints.title: Problem 11.34
hints.question: Calcium phosphate, the main mineral in bones and tooth enamel, precipitates when solutions of calcium chloride and sodium phosphate are mixed: 3 CaCl 2 (aq) + 2 Na 3 PO 4 (aq) → Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 (s) + 6 NaCl(aq) (a) What volume of 0.100 M Na 3 PO 4 reacts completely with 30.0 mL of 0.150 M CaCl 2 ? (b) What mass of Ca 3 (PO 4 ) 2 (310.17 g/mol) forms?
hints.answer: Moles of CaCl 2 : 0.0300 L × 0.150 M = 4.50 × 10 −3 mol. (a) \( 4.50 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol CaCl}_2 \times \dfrac{2\ \text{mol Na}_3\text{PO}_4}{3\ \text{mol CaCl}_2} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{L}}{0.100\ \text{mol Na}_3\text{PO}_4} = 0.0300\ \text{L} = 30.0\ \text{mL} \) (b) \( 4.50 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol CaCl}_2 \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mol Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2}{3\ \text{mol CaCl}_2} \times \dfrac{310.17\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}} = 0.465\ \text{g} \) (a) 30.0 mL ; (b) 0.465 g . The volumes happen to be equal: the Na 3 PO 4 solution is two-thirds as concentrated, and two-thirds as many moles are needed.
hints.hint: Start on the side with both V and M: moles of CaCl<sub>2</sub>. (a) Mole ratio 2 Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> : 3 CaCl<sub>2</sub>, then ÷ molarity. (b) Ratio 1 : 3, then molar mass.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hints.question: Nitrate in a Valley well is measured at 52 mg/L. The drinking water limit is 45 mg/L (as nitrate). Express the measurement in ppm and decide whether it meets the limit.
hints.answer: 52 mg/L ≈ 52 ppm, above the 45 ppm limit.
hints.hint: In dilute water solutions, 1 ppm ≈ 1 mg/L. Convert, then compare with the limit.

hints.title: Problem 12.44
hints.question: Which mixture is a buffer? A. HCl and NaCl B. NH 3 and NaOH C. HNO 2 and NaNO 3 D. HCN and KCN
hints.answer: D. HCN (hydrocyanic acid) is a weak acid, and KCN supplies CN − , its conjugate base. The two differ by exactly one H + . A is a strong acid with its salt. Cl − is too weak a base to take back protons, so nothing in the mixture can neutralize added acid. B is a weak base with a strong base, not with its conjugate acid. NH 3 's partner would be NH 4 + (from NH 4 Cl), and nothing here neutralizes added base. C is a near miss: HNO 2 is weak, but NO 3 − (nitrate) is not its conjugate base. The partner of HNO 2 is NO 2 − (nitrite), from NaNO 2 .
hints.hint: A buffer needs a weak acid with its own conjugate base (the same formula, one H<sup>+</sup> less). Cross out strong acids first, then check each partner.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: Ibuprofen's structure has a –COOH group; ethyl acetate (a nail-polish remover solvent) is an ester, CH 3 –COO–CH 2 CH 3 ; amphetamine has an –NH 2 group. Classify each as an acid, a base, or neither.
hints.answer: Ibuprofen: acid (–COOH). Ethyl acetate: neither (an ester has no acidic H and no amine). Amphetamine: base (amine nitrogen accepts a proton).
hints.hint: Look for the functional group: –COOH means acid, an amine nitrogen (–NH<sub>2</sub>) means base, and an ester (–COO– between carbons) has neither.

hints.title: Problem 12.56
hints.question: What is the conjugate base of the dihydrogen phosphate ion, H 2 PO 4 − ? A. HPO 4 2− B. PO 4 3− C. H 3 PO 4 D. HPO 4 −
hints.answer: A. A conjugate base is one rung down the proton ladder: remove one H + (one H, and the charge goes down by 1). H 3 PO 4 ↔ H 2 PO 4 − ↔ HPO 4 2− ↔ PO 4 3− . B removes two protons, two rungs down. A conjugate is always one H + away. C adds a proton: H 3 PO 4 is the conjugate acid of H 2 PO 4 − . D removes the H but forgets to change the charge. Removing H + takes a positive charge away, so −1 becomes −2.
hints.hint: A conjugate base is one rung down the proton ladder: one fewer H, and the charge goes down by 1.

hints.title: Problem 12.5
hints.question: Write a balanced molecular equation for each neutralization, and name the salt: (a) hydroiodic acid with lithium hydroxide; (b) hydrochloric acid with barium hydroxide. (c) Write the net ionic equation that the two reactions share.
hints.answer: (a) HI(aq) + LiOH(aq) → LiI(aq) + H 2 O(l)    salt: lithium iodide (b) 2 HCl(aq) + Ba(OH) 2 (aq) → BaCl 2 (aq) + 2 H 2 O(l)    salt: barium chloride In (b), Ba(OH) 2 supplies two OH − , so it needs two HCl and makes two waters. Each salt is the base's cation with the acid's anion. (c) H + (aq) + OH − (aq) → H 2 O(l) All four reactants are strong electrolytes, so Li + , I − , Ba 2+ , and Cl − are spectator ions. In (b) the equation H + + OH − → H 2 O happens twice for every Ba(OH) 2 .
hints.hint: The salt is the base's cation with the acid's anion; Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> has two OH<sup>−</sup>, so it needs two acid molecules. For (c), cross out the spectator ions.

hints.title: Problem 12.3
hints.question: A strip of aluminum foil is dropped into hydrochloric acid. (a) Write the balanced equation. (b) Describe what you would see. (c) Which property of acids does this reaction show?
hints.answer: (a) 2 Al(s) + 6 HCl(aq) → 2 AlCl 3 (aq) + 3 H 2 (g) Check: 2 Al, 6 H, and 6 Cl on each side. Aluminum forms Al 3+ , so each Al needs three Cl − , and the six H atoms leave as three H 2 molecules. (b) Bubbles of a colorless gas (hydrogen) form on the metal, and the foil slowly dissolves. The solution may get warm. (c) Acids react with active metals to make hydrogen gas , a single-displacement reaction (Section 7.8), which is why acids corrode metals.
hints.hint: (a) Acid + active metal → salt + hydrogen gas; aluminum forms Al<sup>3+</sup>. (b) Think about the gas and the metal. (c) Compare with the list of acid properties in 12.1.

hints.title: Problem 12.43
hints.question: A student says, "0.010 M lactic acid has pH 2.00, the same as 0.010 M HCl." Which statement about the pH of 0.010 M lactic acid is correct? A. It is exactly 2.00, because [H 3 O + ] equals the acid's molarity. B. It is less than 2.00, because lactic acid is a larger molecule. C. It is greater than 2.00 (but below 7), because lactic acid ionizes only slightly. D. It is 12.00, because a weak acid makes a basic solution.
hints.answer: C. Lactic acid is weak, so [H 3 O + ] is much less than 0.010 M. A smaller [H 3 O + ] means a higher pH, so the pH is above 2.00, while the solution is still acidic. A treats the weak acid as fully ionized. [H 3 O + ] = molarity holds only for strong acids, such as the HCl. B has no basis: the size of the molecule does not raise [H 3 O + ]. A pH below 2.00 would need more H 3 O + than a fully ionized acid gives, which is impossible here. D confuses "weak" with "basic." A weak acid is still an acid; it just raises [H 3 O + ] less. (12.00 is 14.00 − 2.00, a pOH-style slip.)
hints.hint: Is lactic acid strong or weak? A weak acid makes less H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> than its molarity; does less H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> mean a higher or a lower pH?

hints.title: Problem 12.8
hints.question: Which statement is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of a base? A. A substance that donates a proton (H + ) B. A substance that produces OH − ions when it dissolves in water C. A substance that accepts a proton (H + ) D. Any substance whose formula contains hydrogen
hints.answer: C. Brønsted–Lowry bases are proton acceptors ("BAD": bases accept, acids donate). A is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of an acid . B is the Arrhenius definition of a base. It is narrower: it misses bases such as NH 3 that contain no hydroxide. D is a common trap. NH 3 and CH 4 both contain H, and neither donates it in water; having H atoms does not decide anything.
hints.hint: Remember BAD: Bases Accept, Acids Donate. Which choice is the Brønsted–Lowry base definition, and which is the older Arrhenius one?

hints.title: Problem 12.48
hints.question: A 1.00 L phosphate buffer contains 0.050 mol H 2 PO 4 − and 0.050 mol HPO 4 2− . (a) Which partner reacts when HCl is added? Write the reaction. (b) If 0.030 mol HCl is added, how many moles of each partner are left? Is the solution still a buffer? (c) If instead 0.070 mol HCl is added, what is left over, and what happens to the pH? (Ignore the small change in volume, and the H + from the weak acid.)
hints.answer: (a) HPO 4 2− (aq) + H 3 O + (aq) → H 2 PO 4 − (aq) + H 2 O(l) (a) The base partner, HPO 4 2− , reacts with the added acid, 1 mol for each mole of H 3 O + . (b) HPO 4 2− : 0.050 − 0.030 = 0.020 mol . H 2 PO 4 − : 0.050 + 0.030 = 0.080 mol . Both partners are still present, so it is still a buffer , and the pH has changed only a little. (c) All 0.050 mol of HPO 4 2− is used up, and 0.070 − 0.050 = 0.020 mol of strong acid is left over. The buffer capacity has been exceeded. The leftover strong acid sets [H 3 O + ] at about 0.020 mol ÷ 1.00 L = 0.020 M, so the pH drops sharply, to about −log(0.020) = 1.70 .
hints.hint: (a) Added acid reacts with the base partner, 1 : 1. (b) Subtract from one partner and add to the other. (c) What happens to the extra acid once the base partner runs out?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hints.question: An arterial blood sample has [H 3 O + ] = 3.16 × 10 −8 M. What is the pH, and is this acidosis, alkalosis, or normal (7.35–7.45)?
hints.answer: pH = −log(3.16 × 10 −8 ) = 7.5003… = 7.500 (three decimal places for three significant figures). Above 7.45: alkalosis . (Context only; interpretation follows the provider's orders.)
hints.hint: pH = −log[H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]; three significant figures give three decimal places. Then compare the pH with 7.35–7.45.

hints.title: Problem 12.12
hints.question: In the reaction below, which two species form a conjugate acid–base pair? NH 4 + (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ NH 3 (aq) + H 3 O + (aq) A. NH 4 + and H 2 O B. NH 4 + and NH 3 C. H 2 O and NH 3 D. NH 4 + and H 3 O +
hints.answer: B. NH 4 + donates a proton and becomes NH 3 ; the two differ by exactly one H + . (The other pair is H 2 O and H 3 O + .) A pairs the two reactants. They are the acid and the base of the forward reaction, not partners; a conjugate pair always has one member on each side. C pairs species that differ by more than one H + (different elements, too). Water's partner here is H 3 O + . D pairs the two acids, one from each side. A pair is an acid with its own conjugate base.
hints.hint: A conjugate pair has one member on each side of the arrow, and the two differ by exactly one H<sup>+</sup>.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: Write (a) the conjugate acid of Cl − ; (b) the conjugate acid and the conjugate base of H 2 PO 4 − .
hints.answer: (a) HCl: Cl − has no H to give, so add one (Cl − + H 2 O ⇄ HCl + OH − on paper; it barely happens). (b) One rung up the ladder, H 3 PO 4 ; one rung down, HPO 4 2− .
hints.hint: (a) Add one H<sup>+</sup> to Cl<sup>−</sup>. (b) Add one H<sup>+</sup> for the conjugate acid and remove one for the conjugate base, changing the charge by 1 each time.

hints.title: Problem 12.37
hints.question: Complete the table. For each solution, give [H 3 O + ], [OH − ], pH, and pOH, and classify it as acidic, basic, or neutral. A dash marks each value you need to find. Fill-in table: four ways to describe acidity Solution [H 3 O + ] (M) [OH − ] (M) pH pOH Acidic, basic, or neutral? (a) 2.7 × 10 −3 — — — — (b) — 3.6 × 10 −5 — — — (c) — — 6.25 — — (d) — — — 3.40 — (e) — — 7.00 — —
hints.answer: (a) pH = −log(2.7 × 10 −3 ) = 2.5686… = 2.57 ; pOH = 14.00 − 2.57 = 11.43 ; [OH − ] = 1.0 × 10 −14 ÷ 2.7 × 10 −3 = 3.7 × 10 −12 M ; acidic . (b) pOH = −log(3.6 × 10 −5 ) = 4.4437… = 4.44 ; pH = 14.00 − 4.44 = 9.56 ; [H 3 O + ] = 1.0 × 10 −14 ÷ 3.6 × 10 −5 = 2.8 × 10 −10 M ; basic . (c) [H 3 O + ] = 10 −6.25 = 5.6 × 10 −7 M ; pOH = 14.00 − 6.25 = 7.75 ; [OH − ] = 10 −7.75 = 1.8 × 10 −8 M ; acidic (only slightly: pH just below 7). (d) [OH − ] = 10 −3.40 = 4.0 × 10 −4 M ; pH = 14.00 − 3.40 = 10.60 ; [H 3 O + ] = 10 −10.60 = 2.5 × 10 −11 M ; basic . (e) [H 3 O + ] = [OH − ] = 1.0 × 10 −7 M ; pOH = 7.00 ; neutral . Each row checks two ways: pH + pOH = 14.00, and [H 3 O + ][OH − ] = 1.0 × 10 −14 . In (d), a low pOH means a high pH: be careful not to read 3.40 as the pH.
hints.hint: Each row has one known value. Use the loop in 12.5: −log, 10<sup>x</sup>, K<sub>w</sub>, and pH + pOH = 14.00. In (d), the given value is the pOH.

hints.title: Problem 13.53
hints.question: In a two-tub water-transfer model of equilibrium, a 500 mL beaker moves water forward from the "reactant" tub and a 100 mL beaker moves water back from the "product" tub. After many rounds, the water levels stop changing. Which statement is true at that point? A. The reactant tub is empty, because the forward beaker is five times larger. B. Both beakers carry the same volume of water per trip, and the product tub holds more water. C. Both tubs hold the same volume of water. D. Water has stopped moving between the tubs.
hints.answer: B. The levels stop changing only when each forward trip is matched by an equal reverse trip: equal rates. The large forward beaker favors the product tub, so the product tub ends up with more water, but the reactant tub is not empty; once it is shallow, the big beaker cannot fill. A forgets the reverse direction. As the product tub fills, the small beaker carries a full load back every trip, so the reactant tub never runs dry. C confuses equal rates with equal amounts . At equilibrium the amounts are constant, not equal. D describes a static stop. Equilibrium is dynamic: both beakers keep moving water, at the same rate.
hints.hint: The levels stop changing when each forward trip is matched by a reverse trip: equal rates. Do equal rates mean equal amounts?

hints.title: Problem 13.28
hints.question: Nitric oxide and bromine are at equilibrium with nitrosyl bromide in a sealed flask: 2 NO(g) + Br 2 (g) ⇄ 2 NOBr(g) More Br 2 is added, and the temperature is kept constant. What happens? A. The equilibrium shifts left, toward the added Br 2 ; K does not change. B. The equilibrium shifts right; K does not change. C. The equilibrium shifts right, and K increases. D. Nothing happens, because the system was already at equilibrium.
hints.answer: B. Add → away: Br 2 is a reactant, so the system shifts away from it, to the right. The extra Br 2 means more forward collisions, so for a while the forward reaction runs faster, using up some Br 2 and NO and making more NOBr. The temperature did not change, so K stays the same; the concentrations rearrange until their ratio equals the same K again. A shifts toward the added substance. Adding pushes the system away from it. C has the right direction, but only a temperature change changes K. D is wrong because adding Br 2 disturbs the equilibrium. Le Chatelier's principle is about exactly that: how an equilibrium responds to a stress.
hints.hint: Add → Away: Br<sub>2</sub> is a reactant. Then remember that only a temperature change changes K.

hints.title: Problem 13.40
hints.question: Oxygen binding to hemoglobin releases heat: Hb(aq) + O 2 (aq) ⇄ HbO 2 (aq) + heat Hard-working muscle is slightly warmer than the rest of the body. What does the extra warmth do to this equilibrium in the muscle? A. It shifts right, so hemoglobin holds its oxygen more tightly. B. Nothing, because temperature changes only the rate, not the equilibrium. C. It shifts left and K decreases, so hemoglobin releases more O 2 where it is needed. D. It shifts left, but K does not change, because the body's temperature is controlled.
hints.answer: C. Heat is a product here (the binding is exothermic). Warming adds heat. Add → away: the system shifts left, HbO 2 gives up O 2 , and K for binding gets smaller. This is one of the reasons active muscle, which is warmer and makes more CO 2 and acid, receives more oxygen. A puts the shift toward the heat that was added, as if adding a product pulled the system toward it. B is wrong because temperature changes both the rates and the equilibrium; it is the one stress that changes K. D has the right direction, but any change in temperature, even a small, local one, changes K.
hints.hint: Heat is a product here. Warming adds heat: Add → Away. Remember that any temperature change changes K.

hints.title: Problem 13.6
hints.question: A patient's temperature rises from 37.0 °C to 39.5 °C during a fever. (a) Use collision theory to explain why her metabolic rate, and with it her heart rate and breathing rate, goes up. (b) The body's reactions are catalyzed by enzymes. Explain why a very high body temperature, above about 41 °C, slows some of these reactions instead of speeding them up. (c) What do the words "optimum temperature" mean for an enzyme?
hints.answer: (a) Higher temperature means faster-moving molecules. The substrate molecules collide with enzymes more often, and a larger fraction of those collisions have enough energy to react, so the enzyme-catalyzed reactions of metabolism run faster. The body then uses oxygen and fuel faster, so the heart pumps faster and she breathes faster to keep up. (b) Enzymes are proteins, and they work only when they hold their exact shape. At too high a temperature the shape begins to change (the enzyme denatures ), the substrate no longer fits, and the catalyzed path with its lower activation energy is lost. The reaction falls back toward its slow, uncatalyzed rate. (c) The optimum temperature is the temperature at which the enzyme works fastest: warm enough for frequent, energetic collisions, but not so hot that the enzyme loses its shape. For most human enzymes it is close to body temperature. (Context only; this is not guidance on treating a fever.)
hints.hint: (a) Apply both effects of a higher temperature on collisions. (b) Enzymes are proteins that need their exact shape. (c) Think of the balance between faster collisions and losing that shape.

hints.title: Problem 13.48
hints.question: A sealed flask that starts with 0.0400 M N 2 O 4 and no NO 2 is held at a constant temperature: N 2 O 4 (g) ⇄ 2 NO 2 (g)    ΔH = +57.2 kJ After 10 s, [N 2 O 4 ] has fallen to 0.0300 M; after 20 s, to 0.0250 M; and after 30 s it reaches 0.0230 M, where it stays. (a) What is [NO 2 ] at 10 s, 20 s, and 30 s? (b) At 10 s, which rate is larger, forward or reverse? At 40 s? (c) Calculate K at this temperature. (d) At 100 °C, K for this reaction is about 0.36. Was this experiment run above or below 100 °C? Explain using ΔH.
hints.answer: (a) Each mole of N 2 O 4 that reacts makes 2 mol of NO 2 , so [NO 2 ] rises by twice the drop in [N 2 O 4 ]: at 10 s, 2 × (0.0400 − 0.0300) = 0.0200 M ; at 20 s, 2 × (0.0400 − 0.0250) = 0.0300 M ; at 30 s, 2 × (0.0400 − 0.0230) = 0.0340 M . (b) At 10 s the concentrations are still changing (N 2 O 4 falling, NO 2 rising), so the forward rate is larger. At 40 s the concentrations are constant, so the system is at equilibrium and the two rates are equal . Notice that the equilibrium concentrations, 0.0230 M and 0.0340 M, are not equal. (c) \( K = \dfrac{[\text{NO}_2]^2}{[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]} = \dfrac{(0.0340)^2}{0.0230} = \dfrac{0.001156}{0.0230} = 0.0503 \) (c) K = 0.0503 (three significant figures). Without the exponent, 0.0340 ÷ 0.0230 = 1.48, which is wrong. (d) Below 100 °C. ΔH is positive, so heat is a reactant, and raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium right and makes K larger. This experiment's K (0.0503) is smaller than K at 100 °C (0.36), so it must have been run at a lower temperature.
hints.hint: (a) Each mole of N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> lost makes 2 mol NO<sub>2</sub>. (b) Are the concentrations still changing? (c) Square [NO<sub>2</sub>] in K. (d) ΔH is positive: does heating make K larger or smaller?

hints.title: Problem 13.30
hints.question: Use the cobalt equilibrium from Section 13.2's problems. The forward reaction is endothermic. [Co(H 2 O) 6 ] 2+ (aq, pink) + 4 Cl − (aq) ⇄ [CoCl 4 ] 2− (aq, blue) + 6 H 2 O(l)    ΔH positive A test tube of the purple equilibrium mixture is divided into four tubes. Predict the shift and the color change for each: (a) concentrated HCl is added, which supplies Cl − ; (b) silver nitrate is added, which removes Cl − as solid AgCl; (c) the tube is placed in an ice bath; (d) the tube is placed in boiling water. (e) In which tubes does K change?
hints.answer: (a) Add a reactant (Cl − ): shift right , more [CoCl 4 ] 2− , so the solution turns blue . (b) Ag + (aq) + Cl − (aq) → AgCl(s) removes Cl − . Take → toward: shift left , more [Co(H 2 O) 6 ] 2+ , so the solution turns pink (with white AgCl solid). (c) ΔH is positive, so heat is a reactant: heat + [Co(H 2 O) 6 ] 2+ + 4 Cl − ⇄ [CoCl 4 ] 2− + 6 H 2 O. Cooling removes heat, so the system shifts left , toward the heat term: pink . (d) Heating adds a reactant (heat): shift right : blue . (e) Only (c) and (d) , the temperature changes. K decreases in the ice bath and increases in boiling water. Adding or removing Cl − shifts the equilibrium but leaves K the same.
hints.hint: (a)(b) Add → Away, Take → Toward for Cl<sup>−</sup>. (c)(d) ΔH is positive, so write heat as a reactant. Pink is on the left, blue on the right. (e) Only one kind of stress changes K.

hints.title: Problem 13.44
hints.question: In red blood cells, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ H 2 CO 3 (aq). Which statement about the enzyme is correct? A. It makes the reaction reach equilibrium faster in both directions, without changing the equilibrium amounts or K. B. It shifts the equilibrium toward H 2 CO 3 , because it speeds up the forward reaction. C. It increases K, so more H 2 CO 3 is present at equilibrium. D. It is used up as the reaction runs, so red blood cells must keep making more of it.
hints.answer: A. A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and the reverse reactions, so it speeds both up by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached much sooner, but the equilibrium mixture and K are the same. That lets the blood switch quickly between making H 2 CO 3 in the tissues and releasing CO 2 in the lungs, in whichever direction the conditions push. B forgets that the enzyme speeds up the reverse reaction just as much as the forward one, so neither direction wins. C is wrong because only temperature changes K; a catalyst changes the path, not the starting and ending points. D is wrong because a catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged and is used over and over.
hints.hint: A catalyst lowers the hill for both the forward and the reverse reactions. Does it change how fast equilibrium is reached, where it ends up, or both?

hints.title: Problem 13.34
hints.question: Mateo Herrera, the irrigation technician with asthma from the chapter opener, is in the first hour of an asthma attack and is breathing fast. Which describes the effect on the blood equilibrium below? CO 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) ⇄ H 2 CO 3 (aq) ⇄ H + (aq) + HCO 3 − (aq) A. It shifts left; [H + ] decreases; blood pH rises. B. It shifts right; [H + ] increases; blood pH falls. C. It shifts left; [H + ] decreases; blood pH falls. D. It does not shift, because water is a pure liquid and is left out of K.
hints.answer: A. Fast breathing blows off CO 2 faster than his cells make it, so CO 2 is removed. Take → toward: the system shifts left, toward CO 2 . H + combines with HCO 3 − to replace the lost CO 2 , so [H + ] drops, and a lower [H + ] means a higher pH (Chapter 12): a mild respiratory alkalosis, as in his blood gas in Section 13.4. B is the direction for CO 2 building up (hypoventilation), not for fast breathing that removes it. C gets the shift and [H + ] right but the pH backward. Fewer H + ions means a less acidic blood, so the pH goes up. D misuses the solid-and-liquid rule. Water is left out of K, but the stress here is a change in CO 2 , which is dissolved (aq) and is in the equilibrium. (The case is for learning chemistry only; it is not treatment advice.)
hints.hint: Fast breathing removes CO<sub>2</sub>. Use Take → Toward, then follow [H<sup>+</sup>]: does less H<sup>+</sup> mean a higher or a lower pH?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: Write K for 2 SO 2 (g) + O 2 (g) ⇄ 2 SO 3 (g).
hints.hint: Products over reactants, with each coefficient as an exponent. All three species are gases, so all of them appear.

hints.title: Problem 13.36
hints.question: Fluoride from toothpaste or a fluoride varnish lets enamel rebuild as fluorapatite: Ca 5 (PO 4 ) 3 F(s) ⇄ 5 Ca 2+ (aq) + 3 PO 4 3− (aq) + F − (aq) (a) Saliva supplies Ca 2+ and phosphate ions between meals. Which way does this shift the fluorapatite equilibrium, and is that remineralization or demineralization? (b) Fluorapatite has OH − replaced by F − . Using your answer to the lemon-water problem above, explain why fluorapatite holds up better against acid than hydroxyapatite does. (c) A patient with xerostomia (dry mouth) makes much less saliva. Predict the effect on her enamel.
hints.answer: (a) Ca 2+ and PO 4 3− are products. Add → away: the equilibrium shifts left , and solid mineral forms on the tooth: remineralization . (b) Acid attacks hydroxyapatite mainly by removing OH − (H + + OH − → H 2 O), which pulls the equilibrium toward dissolving. F − is a far weaker base than OH − (Chapter 12), so H + does not remove it nearly as easily. With less of a product being taken away, fluorapatite is shifted toward dissolving much less, so it resists acid better. (H + can still remove some phosphate, so acid can still harm fluorapatite, just less.) (c) With less saliva, less Ca 2+ and phosphate are added and less acid is neutralized, so the equilibrium stays shifted toward demineralization for more of the day, and her risk of caries (tooth decay) rises. (Context only; follow the dentist's treatment plan.)
hints.hint: (a) Ca<sup>2+</sup> and phosphate are products: Add → Away. (b) Which is the weaker base, F<sup>−</sup> or OH<sup>−</sup>, and so harder for H<sup>+</sup> to remove? (c) Less saliva: fewer ions added, less acid neutralized.

hints.title: Problem 13.5
hints.question: A student drops marble chips (calcium carbonate) into hydrochloric acid and watches the bubbles of carbon dioxide: CaCO 3 (s) + 2 HCl(aq) → CaCl 2 (aq) + H 2 O(l) + CO 2 (g) Which change makes the bubbling slower ? A. Warming the acid from 20 °C to 40 °C B. Using a few large chips instead of many small chips of the same total mass C. Using 2.0 M HCl instead of 1.0 M HCl D. Grinding the chips into a powder before adding them
hints.answer: B. The reaction happens only where acid touches the surface of the solid. A few large chips expose much less surface area than many small chips of the same mass, so fewer CaCO 3 units are available to collide with the acid each second, and the reaction slows. A speeds the reaction up: hotter particles collide more often and harder, and more collisions have at least E a . C speeds it up: more H + ions per liter means more collisions with the solid per second. D speeds it up a great deal: a powder has far more surface area than chips.
hints.hint: Three of the changes speed the reaction up. Which one reduces how much of the solid's surface can touch the acid?

hints.title: Problem 13.7
hints.question: A package of ground beef is forgotten in a car on a hot afternoon and warms to 33 °C. In the refrigerator it was at 3 °C. (a) Use the rule of thumb that rates about double for every 10 °C to estimate how many times faster the bacteria's enzyme-catalyzed reactions run in the car. (b) Is 33 °C inside the U.S. Department of Agriculture's "danger zone" of 40 °F to 140 °F (about 4 °C to 60 °C)? (c) A friend says, "It's fine; the cold in the refrigerator killed the bacteria anyway." What is wrong with this?
hints.answer: (a) The temperature rose by 33 °C − 3 °C = 30 °C, which is three 10 °C steps. Each step doubles the rate: 2 × 2 × 2 = about 8 times faster . (This is a rough estimate; real bacterial growth depends on the species.) (b) Yes. 33 °C is well inside 4 °C to 60 °C, where bacteria in food can multiply quickly. (c) Cold slows the bacteria's reactions; it does not kill most of them. Once the meat warms up, their reactions speed up again. That is why food is both kept cold and cooked to a safe temperature.
hints.hint: (a) Count the 10 °C steps between the two temperatures, and double once per step. (b) Compare with 4 to 60 °C. (c) Does cold kill bacteria, or slow their reactions?

hints.title: Problem 14.30
hints.question: The Iceman found in an Alpine glacier in 1991 died about 5300 years ago. Compared with the carbon-14 per gram of carbon in living tissue, how much carbon-14 is in his tissue? A. More than 50% B. Exactly 50% C. 25% D. All of it, 100%, because carbon-14 does not decay while it is frozen in ice
hints.answer: A. 5300 years is a little less than one half-life (5730 years), so less than half of his carbon-14 has decayed. More than 50% remains. B would be true only if exactly one half-life, 5730 years, had passed. C is two half-lives, about 11,000 years, roughly twice his age. D treats nuclear decay like spoilage. Freezing preserved his body, but decay happens inside the nucleus and is not slowed by cold.
hints.hint: Compare 5300 years with the half-life of carbon-14, 5730 years. Less than one half-life means less than half has decayed.

hints.title: Problem 14.9
hints.question: Write a balanced nuclear equation for the beta decay of each radioisotope: (a) strontium-90, a fission product in nuclear waste; (b) hydrogen-3 (tritium), used in glowing exit signs; (c) cesium-137, another fission product (its daughter forms in the metastable state, so write it with an "m").
hints.answer: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and the electron leaves as \( {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \). The mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by 1, one place to the right on the periodic table. (a) \( {}^{90}_{38}\text{Sr} \rightarrow {}^{90}_{39}\text{Y} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \) (b) \( {}^{3}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{3}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \) (c) \( {}^{137}_{55}\text{Cs} \rightarrow {}^{137\text{m}}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \) (a) Strontium (38) becomes yttrium-90 (39). (b) Hydrogen (1) becomes helium-3 (2). (c) Cesium (55) becomes barium-137m (56), which then gives off a gamma ray. Check each: the top numbers match (90, 3, 137), and the bottom numbers add up: 39 + (−1) = 38, 2 + (−1) = 1, 56 + (−1) = 55.
hints.hint: In beta decay the top number stays the same and Z goes up by 1. Find each parent's Z, add 1, and look up the new element.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hints.question: A technologist receives a dose rate of 20. μSv/h standing 1.0 m from a patient who just received a tracer. What is the dose rate at 2.0 m? At 3.0 m?
hints.hint: Use the inverse-square law: doubling the distance cuts the dose rate to one-fourth; tripling it cuts it to one-ninth.

hints.title: Problem 14.15
hints.question: Technetium-99m gives off a gamma ray: \( {}^{99\text{m}}_{43}\text{Tc} \rightarrow {}^{99}_{43}\text{Tc} + {}^{0}_{0}\gamma \). Which statement about this change is correct? A. The mass number drops by 1, because the gamma ray carries away part of the nucleus. B. The technetium becomes ruthenium, because the gamma ray raises the atomic number by 1. C. The nucleus releases extra energy; the mass number, atomic number, and element all stay the same. D. The gamma ray is an electron thrown out of the nucleus.
hints.answer: C. A gamma ray is high-energy electromagnetic radiation with mass number 0 and charge 0. The metastable nucleus simply drops to a lower-energy state, so it is still technetium-99, with 43 protons and 56 neutrons. A gives the gamma ray a mass number. It has none, so A stays 99. B gives the gamma ray a charge. With Z = 0 it cannot change the element; raising Z by 1 is beta decay. D describes a beta particle. A gamma ray is light, not a particle with mass or charge.
hints.hint: A gamma ray has mass number 0 and charge 0. What can it change about A, Z, or the element?

hints.title: Problem 14.45
hints.question: A patient who has received iodine-131 therapy (half-life 8.0 days) gives off gamma rays. Suppose the dose rate is 24 μSv/h at 1.0 m from the patient (a made-up value for practice). (a) What is the dose rate at 2.0 m? (b) What dose does a nurse receive standing 2.0 m away for 15 min, and how does that compare with standing 1.0 m away for the same time? (c) Ignoring the iodine the body eliminates, what is the dose rate at 1.0 m 8.0 days later?
hints.answer: (a) \( 24\ \mu\text{Sv/h} \times \tfrac{1}{4} = 6.0\ \mu\text{Sv/h} \)    (twice the distance gives one-fourth the dose rate) (b) \( 6.0\ \tfrac{\mu\text{Sv}}{\text{h}} \times 0.25\ \text{h} = 1.5\ \mu\text{Sv} \qquad \text{at 1.0 m:}\ 24\ \tfrac{\mu\text{Sv}}{\text{h}} \times 0.25\ \text{h} = 6.0\ \mu\text{Sv} \) (a) 6.0 μSv/h ; (b) 1.5 μSv , one-fourth of the 6.0 μSv she would get at 1.0 m (15 min = 0.25 h). Distance and time both lower the dose. (c) 8.0 days is one half-life, so the dose rate is about 24 × 1/2 = 12 μSv/h , and really less, because the body also eliminates iodine in urine, saliva, and sweat. (Context only; care follows the order and the facility's radiation safety protocol.)
hints.hint: (a) Inverse-square law: twice the distance gives one-fourth the dose rate. (b) Dose = dose rate × time; convert minutes to hours. (c) How many half-lives is 8.0 days?

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hints.question: Phosphorus-31 (15 protons, 16 neutrons) is stable. (a) Phosphorus-32 has one extra neutron. Which kind of decay would you expect, and what element forms? (b) Phosphorus-30 has one neutron too few. Which kind of decay would you expect?
hints.answer: (a) Too many neutrons: beta decay, in which a neutron becomes a proton. Z goes from 15 to 16, so sulfur-32 forms (Section 14.2, Example 6). (b) Too few neutrons: positron emission (or electron capture), in which a proton becomes a neutron, giving silicon-30.
hints.hint: Compare each isotope with the stable P-31. Which decay turns a neutron into a proton, and which turns a proton into a neutron? Then find the new Z on the periodic table.

hints.title: Problem 14.42
hints.question: Where does the energy released in nuclear fission come from? A. The uranium burns with oxygen inside the reactor. B. The products have slightly less mass than the reactants, and the missing mass is converted to energy (E = mc 2 ). C. The products have more mass than the reactants, and energy is created along with the new mass. D. All of it comes from the energy of the neutron that starts the fission.
hints.answer: B. Adding up the masses very precisely, the fission fragments and neutrons weigh a little less than the uranium-235 and the neutron that started the fission. Because c 2 is so large, that tiny mass becomes an enormous energy, millions of times more per gram than burning coal or natural gas. A describes a chemical reaction. A reactor burns nothing; fission is a change in the nucleus. C has the mass change backward. Mass is lost, not gained, when energy is released. D cannot be right, because the neutron that starts fission is a slow neutron with very little energy, yet each fission releases a huge amount.
hints.hint: Fission is a nuclear change, not burning. Compare the total mass of the products with the reactants: which way does it change when energy is released?

hints.title: Problem 14.41
hints.question: An operator at a nuclear power plant needs to slow the chain reaction in the reactor core. Which part of the reactor does she adjust, and how? A. She lowers the control rods further into the core, because they absorb neutrons. B. She lowers more fuel rods into the core, because extra uranium absorbs the extra neutrons. C. She raises the control rods out of the core, because they release neutrons. D. She opens the containment building, so neutrons can escape into the air.
hints.answer: A. Control rods are made of neutron-absorbing elements such as boron or cadmium. The deeper they sit in the core, the more neutrons they absorb, so fewer neutrons are left to cause new fissions. B mixes up fuel rods and control rods. More uranium-235 would make more fissions and speed the reaction up. C has the rods backward: raising them out of the core lets more neutrons cause fissions, which speeds up the reaction. Control rods absorb neutrons; they do not release them. D would release radioactive material. The containment building exists to keep it inside.
hints.hint: Control rods absorb neutrons. To slow the chain reaction, should more or fewer neutrons be absorbed?

hints.title: Problem 14.35
hints.question: Hydrogen-3 (tritium, half-life 12.3 years) is used to estimate how long ago groundwater fell as rain. Water from a deep well has 12.5% of the tritium found in rain from the same region. About how many years ago did the water fall as rain? (Assume the tritium in rain has stayed the same.)
hints.answer: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% is 3 half-lives. \( \text{time} = 3 \times 12.3\ \text{years} = 36.9\ \text{years} \) 36.9 years . The same half-life reasoning works for any isotope; the choice of isotope depends on the age being measured. Tritium's short half-life suits water a few decades old, where carbon-14 would show almost no change.
hints.hint: Make a percent arrow map from the rain value down to 12.5% and count the arrows. Multiply by tritium's half-life.

hints.title: Problem 14.23
hints.question: A lab measures the activity of a radioisotope sample every 15.0 hours. The table below shows the results. Activity of a radioisotope sample over time Time (h) Activity (mCi) 0 96.0 15.0 48.0 30.0 24.0 45.0 12.0 60.0 6.00 (a) What is the half-life? (b) What will the activity be at 90.0 h? (c) At what time will the activity be 3.00 mCi?
hints.answer: (a) The activity halves in every 15.0-hour step (96.0 → 48.0 → 24.0 …), so the half-life is 15.0 h . (This matches sodium-24, half-life 15.0 h.) (b) \( n = \dfrac{90.0\ \text{h}}{15.0\ \text{h}} = 6 \qquad 96.0\ \text{mCi} \times \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6} = 96.0\ \text{mCi} \times \tfrac{1}{64} = 1.50\ \text{mCi} \) (c) From 6.00 mCi at 60.0 h, one more half-life gives 3.00 mCi: 60.0 h + 15.0 h = 75.0 h . (Or: 96.0 → 3.00 mCi is 5 halvings, and 5 × 15.0 h = 75.0 h.) (a) 15.0 h ; (b) 1.50 mCi ; (c) 75.0 h .
hints.hint: (a) How long does the activity take to fall to half? (b) Count half-lives in 90.0 h and halve from 96.0. (c) Keep halving from the last row of the table.

hints.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hints.question: Oxygen-15 is a positron emitter used in some PET studies of blood flow. Write the balanced nuclear equation.
hints.answer: Oxygen is element 8. A stays 15; Z becomes 8 − 1 = 7, nitrogen: \( {}^{15}_{8}\text{O} \rightarrow {}^{15}_{7}\text{N} + {}^{0}_{+1}\text{e} \).
hints.hint: A positron is <sup>0</sup><sub>+1</sub>e. Keep the top number; the daughter's Z plus 1 must equal oxygen's Z. Look up that element.

hints.title: Problem 14.11
hints.question: Thallium-201, used in some heart scans, decays by electron capture. (a) Write the balanced nuclear equation. (b) Electron capture and positron emission both change the nucleus in the same way. What is that change, and how do the two equations look different?
hints.answer: (a) Thallium is element 81. In electron capture the electron is a reactant , written on the left: \( {}^{201}_{81}\text{Tl} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \rightarrow {}^{201}_{80}\text{Hg} \) Check: top, 201 + 0 = 201; bottom, 81 + (−1) = 80, mercury. (b) In both, a proton becomes a neutron: the mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes down by 1 . In electron capture the nucleus pulls in an inner electron, so \( {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \) appears on the left . In positron emission a positron is thrown out, so \( {}^{0}_{+1}\text{e} \) appears on the right .
hints.hint: (a) In electron capture, write <sup>0</sup><sub>−1</sub>e on the left, as a reactant. (b) Compare what happens to A and Z in each, and which side the electron or positron appears on.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: Write 0.0825 as a percent, and 4.6% as a decimal.
whys.why: Percent means "per hundred," so a decimal becomes a percent by multiplying by 100 and a percent becomes a decimal by dividing by 100.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: Will a fluoride ion, F − , attract or repel (a) a potassium ion, K + ; (b) a chloride ion, Cl − ?
whys.why: K<sup>+</sup> has the opposite sign to F<sup>−</sup>, so they attract; Cl<sup>−</sup> has the same negative sign as F<sup>−</sup>, so they repel.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: How many protons and electrons are in a neutral atom of magnesium?
whys.answer: Mg has Z = 12: 12 protons and 12 electrons.
whys.why: The atomic number gives the protons, and a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so both equal Z.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Which subatomic particle has (a) no charge, (b) almost no mass, (c) a positive charge?
whys.why: The neutron has charge 0, the electron is only about 0.00055 amu, and the proton carries the 1+ charge.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: Name the element in group 2, period 3, and classify it.
whys.answer: Magnesium, Mg: an alkaline earth metal (main group).
whys.why: Group 2 is the alkaline earth metals, and magnesium sits in period 3 of that column.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
whys.question: Without looking: write the symbols for magnesium, sulfur, potassium, and silicon, and name the elements Ne, B, Al, and Cl.
whys.answer: Mg, S, K, Si; neon, boron, aluminum, chlorine.
whys.why: These are among the first 20 elements; potassium's K comes from its Latin name, kalium, and the others come from their English names.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
whys.question: Name the ions F − , K + , and S 2− .
whys.why: Anions take the root plus -ide (fluor- → fluoride, sulf- → sulfide), while a metal cation keeps the element's name, as in potassium ion.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Lithium has two isotopes, lithium-6 and lithium-7, and an average atomic mass of 6.94 amu. Which is more abundant?
whys.answer: Lithium-7: 6.94 is much closer to 7 than to 6.
whys.why: A weighted average sits closest to the most abundant isotope, and 6.94 is much closer to 7 than to 6.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: How many electrons can the third shell (n = 3) hold, and how are they divided among its subshells?
whys.why: Each orbital holds 2 electrons, and 3s, 3p, and 3d have 1, 3, and 5 orbitals, so 2 + 6 + 10 = 18.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Which element has the configuration [Kr] 5s 2 ?
whys.why: Krypton has 36 electrons, so 36 + 2 = 38 = Z, which is strontium, the group 2 element in row 5.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: How many oxygen atoms are in Fe 2 (CO 3 ) 3 ?
whys.why: Each carbonate ion, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, has 3 O, and the subscript 3 after the parentheses means three carbonate groups, so 3 × 3.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: Write the formulas for the compounds of (a) potassium and sulfur; (b) aluminum and chlorine; (c) barium and nitrogen.
whys.why: Each formula has zero total charge: two K<sup>+</sup> balance one S<sup>2−</sup>, three Cl<sup>−</sup> balance one Al<sup>3+</sup>, and three Ba<sup>2+</sup> (6+) balance two N<sup>3−</sup> (6−).

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Write the formulas for (a) magnesium nitrate; (b) sodium phosphate; (c) ammonium carbonate.
whys.why: Mg<sup>2+</sup> needs two NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, three Na<sup>+</sup> balance one PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>, and two NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> balance one CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
whys.question: Name BaCl 2 ·2H 2 O, and write the formula for sodium carbonate decahydrate.
whys.answer: Barium chloride dihydrate. Na 2 CO 3 ·10H 2 O.
whys.why: Barium is a group 2 fixed-charge metal (no numeral) and di- means 2 waters; deca- means 10 waters, written after Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, where two Na<sup>+</sup> balance one CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Write formulas for (a) carbon disulfide; (b) nitrogen triiodide; (c) tetraphosphorus hexoxide.
whys.why: In a molecular compound each prefix is the atom count: carbon has no prefix (1 C) and disulfide means 2 S, triiodide means 3 I, and tetraphosphorus hexoxide means 4 P and 6 O.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Write formulas for (a) nitrogen trifluoride; (b) magnesium nitride; (c) nitric acid; (d) ammonium nitrite.
whys.answer: (a) NF 3 . (b) Mg 3 N 2 . (c) HNO 3 . (d) NH 4 NO 2 .
whys.why: Tri- gives F<sub>3</sub>; three Mg<sup>2+</sup> balance two N<sup>3−</sup>; nitric acid comes from nitrate, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, with one H<sup>+</sup>; and NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> pairs 1 : 1 with nitrite, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: What is the mass of one mole of oxygen molecules , O 2 ? Of oxygen atoms ?
whys.why: Each O<sub>2</sub> molecule holds two O atoms, so a mole of O<sub>2</sub> weighs twice oxygen's atomic mass, while a mole of O atoms weighs the atomic mass itself.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: An acetaminophen tablet contains 325 mg of acetaminophen, C 8 H 9 NO 2 (151.165 g/mol). How many millimoles is that?
whys.why: Grams divided by g/mol gives moles, and 1000 mmol per mol turns that into millimoles; dividing mg by the molar mass read as mg/mmol gives the same result in one step.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: How many moles of nitrogen atoms are in 0.40 mol of Ca(NO 3 ) 2 ?
whys.answer: 0.40 mol × 2 mol N / 1 mol Ca(NO 3 ) 2 = 0.80 mol N.
whys.why: Each formula unit holds two nitrate ions with one N each, so the ratio is 2 mol N per 1 mol Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, which doubles the moles.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Classify each as a salt, a base, or a metal oxide: (a) LiOH; (b) Al 2 O 3 ; (c) CaCO 3 .
whys.why: LiOH contains the hydroxide ion, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is a metal with the oxide ion, and CaCO<sub>3</sub> is a metal cation with a polyatomic anion that is neither OH<sup>−</sup> nor O<sup>2−</sup>.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: What is the mass percent of carbon in carbon dioxide (44.009 g/mol)?
whys.why: Mass percent is the element's mass in one mole (1 × 12.011 g of C) divided by the molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub>, times 100%.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: Give the empirical formula of (a) C 2 H 6 ; (b) N 2 O 4 ; (c) C 6 H 6 ; (d) H 2 O 2 .
whys.why: Each empirical formula is the molecular formula divided by the largest common factor of its subscripts (2, 2, 6 and 2), giving the simplest whole-number ratio.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
whys.question: In a sealed flask, 4.0 g of hydrogen reacts completely with 32.0 g of oxygen. What is the mass of water formed?
whys.answer: 4.0 g + 32.0 g = 36.0 g of water (conservation of mass).
whys.why: Mass is conserved in a sealed flask, so the water's mass equals the total mass of hydrogen and oxygen that reacted.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Balance: Zn(s) + HCl(aq) → ZnCl 2 (aq) + H 2 (g).
whys.why: ZnCl<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> each need 2 Cl and 2 H, so a coefficient of 2 on HCl balances both while Zn is already 1 = 1.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Write the ions formed when Al(NO 3 ) 3 dissolves.
whys.why: Aluminum nitrate is a soluble ionic compound, so it separates into one Al<sup>3+</sup> and three NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ions, which keep their own covalent bonds.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
whys.question: Does Sn(s) react with Al(NO 3 ) 3 (aq)?
whys.answer: No: tin is below aluminum in the series.
whys.why: A free metal displaces only the ions of a metal below it, and aluminum is above tin, so Sn cannot displace Al<sup>3+</sup>.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: For 4 Fe(s) + 3 O 2 (g) → 2 Fe 2 O 3 (s), how many moles of O 2 react with 2.0 mol Fe?
whys.answer: 2.0 mol Fe × 3 mol O 2 / 4 mol Fe = 1.5 mol O 2 .
whys.why: The balanced equation says 3 mol O<sub>2</sub> react for every 4 mol Fe, so multiply the moles of Fe by 3/4.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: For C 3 H 8 + 5 O 2 → 3 CO 2 + 4 H 2 O, how many moles of water form from 0.75 mol propane?
whys.why: One mole of propane makes 4 mol of water (coefficients 1 and 4), so multiply by 4/1; the ratio is exact, so the answer keeps two significant figures like 0.75.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: How many moles of NaOH are in 25.0 mL of 0.200 M NaOH?
whys.why: Molarity is moles per liter, so 0.0250 L × 0.200 mol/L leaves mol NaOH, with three significant figures.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: What volume of CO 2 at STP forms when 0.250 mol of CaCO 3 decomposes? CaCO 3 → CaO + CO 2
whys.why: One mol CaCO<sub>3</sub> gives one mol CO<sub>2</sub>, and at STP each mole of gas fills 22.4 L, so 0.250 mol × 22.4 L/mol gives the volume.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 45.0 g and an actual yield of 38.2 g. What is the percent yield?
whys.why: The actual yield (38.2 g) goes on top and the theoretical yield (45.0 g) on the bottom, so the result is a little below 100%, as expected.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: A 12-oz can of soda provides 155 Cal. Convert this to kilojoules.
whys.why: A food Calorie is 4.184 kJ, so 155 Cal × 4.184 kJ/Cal gives kilojoules, with three significant figures like 155 (the conversion is exact).

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: How much heat is needed to warm 50.0 g of water from 25.0 °C to 80.0 °C?
whys.why: The water warms by 55.0 °C, so q = (50.0 g)(4.184 J/(g·°C))(55.0 °C); q is positive because the water absorbs heat.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: A 15.0 g gold ring absorbs 125 J. By how much does its temperature rise? (c for gold = 0.128 J/(g·°C))
whys.why: Dividing the heat by mass × specific heat leaves only °C: 125 J ÷ (15.0 g × 0.128 J/(g·°C)); gold's low specific heat gives a large rise.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: A white solid melts at 801 °C, does not conduct as a solid, and conducts when dissolved in water. What type of solid is it?
whys.why: Ionic solids have strong ionic bonds (a high melting point) and ions locked in a lattice, so they conduct only when melting or dissolving frees the ions to move.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
whys.question: A blood pressure reading is 118/76 mmHg. Express the systolic value, 118 mmHg, in atm.
whys.why: Since 1 atm = 760 mmHg exactly, dividing by 760 converts mmHg to atm, and the answer keeps the three significant figures of 118 mmHg.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: The gas in a sealed syringe occupies 10.0 mL at 1.00 atm. The plunger is pulled back until the volume is 25.0 mL at the same temperature. What is the new pressure?
whys.why: At constant temperature and moles, Boyle's law gives P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>; the volume grew 2.5 times, so the pressure fell to 1/2.5 of its value.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: A rigid tank of nitrogen is at 2.15 atm at 20.0 °C. What is its pressure at 45.0 °C?
whys.why: With volume and moles constant, pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature, so P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> × T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> with 318.15 K and 293.15 K, and warming raises the pressure.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: What volume do 2.25 mol of N 2 occupy at 1.50 atm and 30.0 °C?
whys.why: With one set of conditions, V = nRT/P, using T = 303.15 K; R = 0.082058 L·atm/(mol·K) with P in atm leaves the answer in liters.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: How many moles of O 2 are in Mateo's 4.70 L portable cylinder at 136 atm and 21.0 °C?
whys.why: n = PV/(RT) with T = 294.15 K; P in atm and V in liters match R = 0.082058 L·atm/(mol·K), so only moles are left.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
whys.question: For 2 CO(g) + O 2 (g) → 2 CO 2 (g), what volume of O 2 is needed to burn 6.00 L of CO, both at the same temperature and pressure?
whys.answer: 6.00 L CO × (1 L O 2 / 2 L CO) = 3.00 L O 2 .
whys.why: At the same T and P, equal volumes hold equal moles (Avogadro's law), so the 1 : 2 coefficient ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to CO is also a volume ratio, and liters go straight to liters.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
whys.question: A drawing of a gas sample shows 9 particles of gas A and 3 particles of gas B at a total pressure of 800. mmHg. What is the partial pressure of B?
whys.why: Every particle contributes equally to the pressure, so B's share of the particles (3 of 12) is its share of the total: P<sub>B</sub> = X<sub>B</sub> × P<sub>total</sub>.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
whys.question: What is the mass percent of sugar in a drink made from 26.0 g of sugar and 224.0 g of water?
whys.why: Mass percent divides the solute by the total mass of solution (26.0 g + 224.0 g = 250.0 g), not by the water alone.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
whys.question: Nitrate in a Valley well is measured at 52 mg/L. The drinking water limit is 45 mg/L (as nitrate). Express the measurement in ppm and decide whether it meets the limit.
whys.answer: 52 mg/L ≈ 52 ppm, above the 45 ppm limit.
whys.why: A liter of dilute water solution has a mass of about 1 kg, so milligrams per liter equal milligrams per kilogram, which is parts per million; 52 ppm is more than the 45 ppm limit.

whys.title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
whys.question: Express 0.00450 M glucose in millimolar.
